title: Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
description: This module introduces students to fundamental graph traversal algorithms that form the backbone of many computational solutions in computer science. Graph algorithms are essential for solving problems in network analysis, pathfinding, social media platforms, web crawling, and artificial intelligence. Students will explore Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithms, understanding their implementation, time and space complexity, and practical applications. The module emphasizes hands-on coding experience with real-world scenarios such as finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs, detecting cycles, and exploring connected components. Through interactive coding exercises and visual demonstrations, students will develop intuition for when to apply each algorithm and how graph representation affects performance. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in algorithms, network theory, and machine learning, while building critical problem-solving skills that directly transfer to technical interviews and software development roles.
key_concepts: Breadth-First Search (BFS) - systematic level-by-level graph exploration using queues, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs
Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive graph exploration that goes as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for topological sorting and cycle detection
Graph representations - adjacency lists and adjacency matrices with their respective memory usage and access time trade-offs
Queue and Stack data structures - FIFO and LIFO mechanisms that enable BFS and DFS implementations respectively
Time complexity analysis - O(V + E) performance characteristics where V represents vertices and E represents edges
learning_objectives: Students will implement both BFS and DFS algorithms in Python by writing complete, working code that traverses adjacency lists and adjacency matrices
Students will analyze algorithm efficiency through calculating and comparing time and space complexity of BFS versus DFS for different graph structures
Students will solve real-world problems using appropriate graph traversal algorithms, including shortest path finding, cycle detection, and connected component identification
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 22 'Elementary Graph Algorithms' (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 594-630
Journal article: 'Graph Traversal Algorithms and Their Applications' (Zhang & Kumar, 2023) - focus on sections 2.1-2.3 covering BFS/DFS optimizations
Online resource: VisuAlgo Graph Traversal - interactive BFS/DFS visualizations and step-through examples
LeetCode Problems: #200 Number of Islands, #133 Clone Graph - practical algorithm application exercises

title: Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables offer average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for efficient algorithm design and system implementation. Students will examine the mathematical foundations of hash functions, analyze different collision resolution techniques, and implement working hash table solutions. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical application, covering real-world scenarios where hash tables are critical, such as database indexing, caching systems, compiler symbol tables, and password storage. Students will gain hands-on experience with various hashing algorithms, load factor management, and performance optimization techniques. By the end of this module, learners will understand when and how to effectively utilize hash tables in software development, recognize trade-offs between different implementation strategies, and be able to design custom hash functions for specific use cases. This knowledge is crucial for technical interviews, system design, and building scalable software applications.
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps input data to fixed-size integer values, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor - The ratio of occupied slots to total slots in a hash table, critical for maintaining performance and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees about expected collision behavior
Open Addressing - Collision resolution method where colliding elements are stored in alternative locations within the same array using probing sequences

Students will learn how hash tables achieve O(1) average-case performance for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations through effective hash function design and collision resolution techniques. The module covers the mathematical foundations of hashing, practical implementation considerations, and real-world applications ranging from database indexing to compiler symbol tables. Students will implement multiple collision resolution strategies including separate chaining and open addressing variants (linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing). Through hands-on coding exercises and performance analysis, students will understand the trade-offs between different approaches and learn to select appropriate hashing strategies based on specific use cases. This knowledge is essential for system design interviews, optimizing application performance, and understanding the underlying mechanisms of programming language features like dictionaries, sets, and associative arrays.
key_concepts: Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute data uniformly across the hash table
Load Factor - Ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical metric affecting performance and collision frequency
Separate Chaining - Collision resolution method using linked lists or dynamic arrays at each table position to store multiple elements
Open Addressing - Collision resolution technique that finds alternative positions within the table using probing sequences
Universal Hashing - Family of hash functions with mathematical guarantees about collision probability for any input set
learning_objectives: Students will implement hash tables with separate chaining and linear probing by coding complete data structures in Python with insertion, deletion, and search operations
Students will analyze collision resolution performance through empirical testing of load factors and hash function quality metrics
Students will design custom hash functions using mathematical techniques like polynomial rolling hash and multiplication method for specific data types
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 11 Hash Tables (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 253-280
Journal article: Robin Hood Hashing should be your default Hash Table implementation (Celis, 2013) - focuses on variance reduction in open addressing
Online resource: Python.org Documentation - dict implementation details and hash() function specification

title: Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
description: Feature engineering is often considered the cornerstone of successful machine learning projects, yet it remains one of the most underemphasized skills in traditional data science education. This module provides a comprehensive deep-dive into the art and science of transforming raw data into meaningful features that enhance model performance. Students will explore systematic approaches to creating, selecting, and optimizing features across different data types including numerical, categorical, temporal, and text data. The module emphasizes practical techniques such as polynomial features, interaction terms, binning strategies, encoding methods, and dimensionality reduction. Students will learn to balance the trade-offs between feature complexity and model interpretability while avoiding common pitfalls like data leakage and overfitting. Through hands-on projects using real-world datasets, students will develop intuition for identifying which features drive predictive power and learn to implement automated feature selection pipelines. This module is crucial because effective feature engineering can often improve model performance more significantly than algorithm selection alone, making it an essential skill for any practicing data scientist.

Categorical encoding methods - one-hot encoding, target encoding, and ordinal encoding strategies for converting categorical variables into numerical representations
Dimensionality reduction techniques - PCA, feature selection algorithms (univariate, recursive, and model-based) to reduce feature space while preserving information
Feature interaction and polynomial features - creating new features through mathematical combinations and interactions between existing variables
Data leakage prevention - identifying and avoiding future information bleeding into training data, particularly in temporal datasets

Students will evaluate feature importance and eliminate redundant variables through statistical methods, correlation analysis, and automated selection algorithms including RFE and LASSO regularization

title: Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of shortest path algorithms, fundamental components in computer science that solve optimization problems across diverse applications from GPS navigation to network routing protocols. Students will master three essential algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm for weighted graphs with non-negative edges, the Bellman-Ford algorithm for handling negative weights, and the Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, connecting mathematical concepts to real-world problem-solving. Through hands-on coding exercises, students will implement these algorithms from scratch and analyze their time and space complexities. The content bridges abstract algorithmic thinking with concrete applications in transportation networks, social media platforms, and distributed systems. By examining trade-offs between different approaches, students develop critical thinking skills essential for algorithm selection in professional software development. This module serves as a cornerstone for advanced topics in artificial intelligence, network analysis, and optimization theory.
key_concepts: Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from single source in non-negative weighted graphs with O(V²) or O(E log V) complexity
Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution detecting negative cycles while computing shortest paths in O(VE) time complexity
Floyd-Warshall Algorithm - All-pairs shortest path solution using dynamic programming matrix with O(V³) complexity for dense graphs
Graph Representation - Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list trade-offs for memory usage and algorithm efficiency
Relaxation Process - Edge weight update mechanism central to shortest path computation and convergence proof

Bellman-Ford Algorithm: dynamic programming method to detect negative cycles and find shortest paths in graphs with negative edge weights

Graph algorithms are essential in computer science, powering applications from social network analysis and GPS navigation to network routing and web crawling. Students will learn to represent graphs programmatically, implement core traversal algorithms, and solve real-world pathfinding problems. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, preparing students to recognize when graph-based solutions are appropriate and how to apply them effectively. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, students will develop proficiency in designing efficient solutions for connectivity, reachability, and optimization problems that appear across software engineering, data science, and systems design.
key_concepts: Graph representation - Methods for storing graphs including adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and edge lists with trade-offs analysis
Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-by-level traversal algorithm using queues, applications in shortest unweighted paths and connected components
Depth-First Search (DFS) - Deep exploration using stacks/recursion, applications in cycle detection and topological sorting
Dijkstra's Algorithm - Single-source shortest path algorithm for weighted graphs with non-negative edges using priority queues
Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Shortest path algorithm that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles
learning_objectives: Students will implement BFS and DFS algorithms by writing complete Python functions that traverse adjacency lists and matrices
Students will analyze time and space complexity of graph algorithms through Big-O notation and empirical testing on datasets of varying sizes
Students will solve shortest path problems using Dijkstra's algorithm and identify appropriate use cases for different pathfinding approaches
Students will model real-world scenarios as graph problems through designing representations for social networks, transportation systems, and dependency graphs

Textbook chapter: 'Single-Source Shortest Paths' from Introduction to Algorithms (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 643-684
Research paper: 'A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs' (Dijkstra, 1959) - original shortest path algorithm

title: Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems with Multiple Variables
description: This module introduces students to systems of linear equations, a fundamental concept that bridges algebraic manipulation with practical problem-solving. Students will explore how multiple linear relationships can be analyzed simultaneously to find solutions that satisfy all constraints. The module emphasizes both graphical and algebraic approaches, including substitution, elimination, and matrix methods. Through real-world applications such as business optimization, resource allocation, and mixture problems, students will discover how systems of equations model complex scenarios in economics, engineering, and science. The module progressively builds from simple two-variable systems to more complex three-variable systems, preparing students for advanced topics in linear algebra and optimization. Special attention is given to interpreting solutions in context, including cases with no solution or infinite solutions, helping students develop critical thinking about mathematical modeling and solution validity.
key_concepts: System of linear equations - a collection of two or more linear equations with the same variables that are solved simultaneously
Solution set - the set of all ordered pairs or triples that satisfy all equations in the system simultaneously
Elimination method - a technique for solving systems by adding or subtracting equations to eliminate one variable
Substitution method - solving one equation for a variable and substituting that expression into another equation
Inconsistent system - a system with no solution because the equations represent parallel lines or planes
Dependent system - a system with infinitely many solutions because the equations represent the same line or plane
learning_objectives: Students will solve systems of two and three linear equations by applying substitution, elimination, and graphical methods with 90% accuracy
Students will model real-world problems through creating and solving systems of linear equations using word problem analysis techniques
Students will interpret solution sets using graphical representations and determine whether systems have unique, infinite, or no solutions

Students will master both the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of BSTs, including insertion, deletion, and traversal operations. Students will master the theoretical foundations of BSTs, including their structural properties and ordering constraints, while developing practical implementation skills in both recursive and iterative approaches. The module emphasizes the critical relationship between tree balance and performance, examining best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for common operations. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, students will understand why BSTs serve as the foundation for more advanced tree structures like AVL trees and Red-Black trees. This knowledge is essential for software development roles, technical interviews, and advanced computer science coursework. The module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical programming skills, preparing students to make informed decisions about data structure selection in real-world applications. By the end of this module, students will possess both the analytical tools to evaluate BST performance and the implementation expertise to build robust tree-based solutions.
key_concepts: BST Property: For any node, all values in left subtree are smaller, all values in right subtree are larger, enabling efficient search operations
Tree Traversal Algorithms: Systematic methods (in-order, pre-order, post-order) for visiting every node exactly once with specific ordering guarantees
Structural Balance: The relationship between tree height and node distribution that determines whether operations achieve O(log n) or degrade to O(n) performance
Successor/Predecessor Nodes: Next larger/smaller values in sorted order, critical for implementing deletion operations while maintaining BST property
Tree Rotation Operations: Fundamental restructuring techniques that preserve BST property while modifying tree shape for optimization
learning_objectives: Students will implement complete BST classes with insertion, deletion, and search operations by writing recursive and iterative methods in Python or Java
Students will analyze time and space complexity of BST operations through mathematical proof techniques and empirical testing of balanced vs. unbalanced trees
Students will design efficient tree traversal algorithms using in-order, pre-order, and post-order methods to solve practical problems like expression evaluation and data serialization
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 12 - Binary Search Trees (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein, 4th Edition) pp. 287-317
Research Paper: 'Optimal Binary Search Trees' (Knuth, 1971) - sections on average-case analysis and tree construction
Online Resource: VisuAlgo BST Module - interactive tree operations and complexity visualization exercises

title: Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Students will master the principles of hash function design, understand the mathematical foundations of load factors and performance analysis, and implement multiple collision resolution techniques. Hash tables are critical for database indexing, compiler symbol tables, caching systems, and countless real-world applications where O(1) average-case lookup time is essential. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, covering open addressing methods (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing) and separate chaining approaches. Students will analyze the trade-offs between different collision resolution strategies, understand when hash tables degrade to O(n) performance, and learn to choose appropriate hash functions for different data types. Through hands-on coding exercises and performance benchmarking, students will gain the expertise needed to implement efficient hash-based solutions in software engineering roles and technical interviews.
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices
Load Factor - The ratio of number of stored elements to hash table size, directly affecting collision probability and performance
Linear Probing - An open addressing collision resolution method that searches for the next available slot sequentially
Separate Chaining - A collision resolution technique using linked lists or arrays at each hash table index to store multiple elements
Double Hashing - A collision resolution method using a second hash function to determine probe step size, reducing clustering
learning_objectives: Students will implement hash tables with linear probing, quadratic probing, and separate chaining by coding complete data structures in Python or Java
Students will analyze collision resolution performance through empirical testing of different load factors and hash functions on real datasets
Students will design appropriate hash functions using mathematical principles for integers, strings, and custom objects

description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. description: This module introduces students to linear functions as fundamental mathematical models that describe constant rates of change in real-world situations. key_concepts: Slope: The rate of change between two variables, calculated as rise over run or change in y over change in x
Y-intercept: The point where a line crosses the y-axis, representing the initial value or starting point in many applications

Parallel and perpendicular lines: Lines with the same slope are parallel; lines with slopes that are negative reciprocals are perpendicular

key_concepts: Data Leakage: The inadvertent inclusion of information from the future or target variable in training features, leading to overly optimistic model performance estimates

title: Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Collision Resolution
description: This module explores hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables provide average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for building efficient software systems. Students will examine the mathematical foundations of hash functions, understand different collision resolution strategies, and analyze performance characteristics under various conditions. The module covers practical implementation details including dynamic resizing, load factor management, and real-world applications in databases, caching systems, and programming language implementations. Through hands-on coding exercises, students will implement multiple hash table variants and compare their performance. Understanding hash tables is crucial for technical interviews, system design, and building scalable applications. This module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software engineering skills.
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, ideally distributing inputs uniformly across the hash table
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling cases when different keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
Load Factor - The ratio of stored elements to total table capacity, critical for maintaining optimal performance and determining when to resize
Universal Hashing - A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees on expected performance
Dynamic Resizing - The process of expanding or shrinking hash table capacity while rehashing existing elements to maintain efficiency
learning_objectives: Students will design and implement hash functions by analyzing distribution properties and minimizing collision rates through mathematical evaluation
Students will construct hash tables with different collision resolution strategies through coding exercises in Python and Java
Students will evaluate hash table performance using Big O analysis and empirical testing to optimize real-world applications

Students will explore graph traversal techniques including Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS), then advance to shortest path algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm and the Bellman-Ford algorithm. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, connecting abstract algorithmic concepts to concrete applications such as social network analysis, GPS navigation systems, and network routing protocols. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithm analysis, students will develop proficiency in recognizing when to apply specific graph algorithms and how to implement them efficiently. The module includes complexity analysis, helping students understand the trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches. Real-world case studies demonstrate how major technology companies leverage these algorithms in their systems, from Google's PageRank algorithm to Facebook's friend recommendation systems. By the end of this module, students will have built a solid foundation in graph theory applications that will serve them throughout their computer science careers.
key_concepts: Graph Representation - Understanding adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and their trade-offs for different graph operations
Depth-First Search (DFS) - Recursive and iterative approaches to exploring graph nodes, including applications to cycle detection and topological sorting
Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-order traversal technique for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs and solving connectivity problems
Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach for finding shortest paths from a single source in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights
Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution for shortest paths that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles
Time and Space Complexity - Analyzing algorithm efficiency in terms of vertices (V) and edges (E) for different graph representations
learning_objectives: Students will implement DFS and BFS traversal algorithms by coding complete solutions in Python with proper time and space complexity analysis
Students will solve shortest path problems through hands-on implementation of Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford algorithms on weighted graphs
Students will analyze algorithm efficiency using Big O notation to compare performance characteristics of different graph algorithms
Students will apply graph algorithms to real-world scenarios by completing a capstone project involving network analysis or pathfinding

title: Systems of Linear Equations: Methods and Applications
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of systems of linear equations, focusing on solution methods and real-world applications. Students will master three fundamental algebraic techniques—substitution, elimination, and matrix methods—while developing critical thinking skills to determine when each method is most appropriate. The module emphasizes both computational fluency and conceptual understanding, connecting abstract mathematical procedures to practical problem-solving scenarios in business, engineering, and social sciences. Through guided practice and application problems, students will learn to model multi-variable relationships, interpret solutions in context, and recognize when systems have unique solutions, infinite solutions, or no solution. This foundation is essential for advanced topics in linear algebra, calculus, and applied mathematics, making it a cornerstone module for students pursuing STEM fields or careers requiring quantitative analysis.
key_concepts: System of linear equations - A collection of two or more linear equations with the same variables that are solved simultaneously
Substitution method - Solving technique where one equation is solved for a variable, then substituted into other equations
Elimination method - Process of adding or subtracting equations to eliminate variables systematically
Augmented matrix - A matrix representation combining coefficient matrix with constants column for solving systems
Inconsistent system - A system with no solution where equations represent parallel lines or planes
Dependent system - A system with infinitely many solutions where equations represent the same line or plane

title: Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Techniques
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables offer O(1) average-case performance for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for building efficient software systems. Students will learn how hash functions distribute data across memory, understand the mathematical principles behind collision resolution, and implement various strategies for handling hash collisions. The module covers both theoretical foundations and practical applications, including real-world use cases in databases, compilers, and web applications. Students will analyze the trade-offs between different collision resolution methods, evaluate hash function quality, and understand load factor impacts on performance. This knowledge is crucial for technical interviews, system design, and building scalable applications. By the end of this module, students will have hands-on experience implementing hash tables from scratch and will understand when and why to use them in various computing scenarios.
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing data uniformly across available slots
Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys map to the same hash table index, including chaining and open addressing
Load Factor - The ratio of stored elements to total table capacity, directly affecting performance and collision probability
Separate Chaining - A collision resolution method using linked lists or arrays at each table index to store multiple values
Open Addressing - A collision resolution approach that finds alternative positions within the table using probing sequences
learning_objectives: Students will implement a hash table with linear probing collision resolution by coding a complete class structure with insert, delete, and search methods
Students will analyze hash function performance through calculating distribution uniformity and collision rates using statistical measurements
Students will compare collision resolution strategies using empirical testing of separate chaining, linear probing, and double hashing techniques
Students will evaluate hash table efficiency by measuring load factors and their impact on operation performance through benchmark analysis
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 11 - Hash Tables (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 253-285
Journal article: Universal Hashing and Perfect Hash Functions (Carter & Wegman, 1979) - focus on theoretical foundations
GeeksforGeeks: Hashing Data Structure - comprehensive implementation examples and collision resolution comparisons
Research paper: Robin Hood Hashing (Celis et al., 1985) - advanced open addressing technique analysis

title: Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
description: Dynamic programming is a fundamental algorithmic paradigm that solves complex problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems and storing solutions to avoid redundant computations. This module explores the theoretical foundations and practical applications of dynamic programming, emphasizing the transition from recursive solutions to optimized memoized implementations. Students will master the identification of overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure properties, two key characteristics that make problems suitable for dynamic programming approaches. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, learners will implement classic dynamic programming solutions including the Fibonacci sequence, longest common subsequence, knapsack problems, and matrix chain multiplication. The module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software development skills, demonstrating how dynamic programming reduces exponential time complexity to polynomial time in many real-world scenarios. Understanding dynamic programming is crucial for technical interviews, competitive programming, and developing efficient algorithms in areas such as bioinformatics, operations research, and artificial intelligence. By the end of this module, students will confidently recognize dynamic programming opportunities and implement both top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation) solutions.
key_concepts: Overlapping Subproblems: The property where a recursive algorithm solves the same subproblems multiple times, making it suitable for optimization through storage of intermediate results
Optimal Substructure: The characteristic where an optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems, enabling the build-up of solutions from smaller components

Memoization (Top-Down): A technique that stores the results of expensive function calls and returns cached results when the same inputs occur again, typically implemented using recursion with a lookup table
Tabulation (Bottom-Up): A method that builds solutions iteratively from the smallest subproblems up to the target problem, typically using arrays or matrices to store intermediate results
State Space: The set of all possible configurations or parameters that define unique subproblems in a dynamic programming solution
learning_objectives: Students will identify problems suitable for dynamic programming by recognizing overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure properties through systematic problem analysis
Students will implement both top-down memoized and bottom-up tabulated solutions through hands-on coding exercises in Python and Java
Students will analyze time and space complexity improvements using Big O notation to compare naive recursive solutions with dynamic programming optimizations
Students will solve classic dynamic programming problems including 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, and edit distance through structured coding assignments

title: Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization and Tabulation
description: This module introduces students to dynamic programming, a fundamental algorithmic paradigm that solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing solutions to avoid redundant calculations. Students will explore both top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation) approaches, understanding when and why dynamic programming provides optimal solutions. The module covers classic problems including the Fibonacci sequence, longest common subsequence, knapsack problem, and edit distance. Through hands-on implementation and complexity analysis, students will develop the critical thinking skills needed to recognize dynamic programming opportunities in real-world scenarios. This technique is essential for technical interviews, competitive programming, and optimizing algorithms in software development. Students will learn to identify optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems—the two key properties that make dynamic programming applicable. The module emphasizes practical implementation in Python, with extensions to other programming languages, ensuring students can apply these concepts immediately in their projects and coursework.
key_concepts: Optimal Substructure: Property where optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems
Overlapping Subproblems: Recursive algorithm revisits same subproblems multiple times
Memoization: Top-down approach storing results of expensive function calls in cache
Tabulation: Bottom-up approach building solution iteratively using previously computed values
State Space: Set of all possible states/subproblems in dynamic programming solution
Recurrence Relation: Mathematical formula expressing solution in terms of smaller subproblems
learning_objectives: Students will identify problems suitable for dynamic programming by recognizing optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems through structured problem analysis exercises
Students will implement both memoization and tabulation solutions for classic dynamic programming problems through hands-on coding assignments in Python

title: Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems Using Matrix Methods
description: This module explores the fundamental concepts and practical applications of systems of linear equations, with emphasis on matrix-based solution methods. Students will master three primary solution techniques: Gaussian elimination, matrix inversion, and Cramer's rule, while understanding when each method is most appropriate. The module bridges abstract algebraic concepts with concrete real-world applications, including economics (supply and demand modeling), engineering (circuit analysis), and business optimization problems. Students will work extensively with augmented matrices, row operations, and determinants to develop both computational fluency and conceptual understanding. Special attention is given to identifying inconsistent and dependent systems, interpreting solutions geometrically, and recognizing the limitations of each solution method. Through guided practice problems progressing from simple 2x2 systems to complex 4x4 applications, students will build confidence in matrix manipulation while developing critical thinking skills about solution strategies. This foundational topic serves as a gateway to advanced linear algebra concepts and prepares students for multivariable calculus applications.
key_concepts: Augmented Matrix: A matrix formed by appending the constant vector to the coefficient matrix, enabling systematic solution of linear systems through row operations
Gaussian Elimination: A systematic algorithm using elementary row operations to transform an augmented matrix into row echelon form for back-substitution solving
Matrix Determinant: A scalar value computed from square matrices that determines system solvability and enables Cramer's rule application for unique solutions
Row Echelon Form: A matrix configuration where leading entries form a step pattern, facilitating systematic back-substitution to find variable values
Cramer's Rule: A formula-based method using determinant ratios to solve systems with unique solutions when the coefficient matrix is invertible

key_concepts: One-sided limits: The behavior of a function as x approaches a value from the left (x → a⁻) or right (x → a⁺) side exclusively
Epsilon-delta definition: The formal mathematical definition stating that lim(x→a) f(x) = L if for every ε > 0, there exists δ > 0 such that |f(x) - L| < ε whenever 0 < |x - a| < δ
Continuity at a point: A function is continuous at x = a if three conditions are met: f(a) exists, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a)
Indeterminate forms: Expressions like 0/0, ∞/∞, or ∞ - ∞ that require special techniques such as factoring, rationalization, or algebraic manipulation to evaluate

title: Linear Transformations and Matrix Representations
description: This module explores the fundamental concept of linear transformations and their matrix representations, bridging abstract linear algebra with practical computational applications. Students will discover how linear transformations preserve vector operations while enabling geometric transformations like rotations, reflections, and scaling. The module emphasizes the powerful connection between abstract mathematical functions and concrete matrix calculations, showing how any linear transformation can be completely characterized by its matrix representation. Through visual demonstrations and computational exercises, students will understand how linear transformations form the backbone of computer graphics, data analysis, and engineering applications. The module builds intuition through geometric interpretations while developing technical skills in matrix operations, eigenvalue analysis, and transformation composition. By connecting theoretical concepts to real-world applications like image processing and 3D graphics, students will appreciate how linear transformations serve as essential tools across STEM fields. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in differential equations, optimization, and machine learning where linear transformations are fundamental.
key_concepts: Linear Transformation: A function T: V → W between vector spaces that preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication (T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u))
Matrix Representation: The unique matrix [T] that encodes a linear transformation T, where each column contains the image of a basis vector under T
Kernel and Image: The kernel (null space) contains vectors mapped to zero; the image (range) contains all possible output vectors of the transformation
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: Special scalars λ and vectors v where T(v) = λv, revealing the transformation's fundamental directional behaviors
learning_objectives: Students will determine whether given functions are linear transformations by verifying preservation of vector addition and scalar multiplication properties
Students will construct matrix representations of linear transformations through systematic calculation of basis vector images and column arrangement
Students will analyze geometric effects of linear transformations using eigenvalue decomposition and determinant calculations

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) with Unit Testing Frameworks
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing code. Students will learn the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, explore different types of testing, and gain hands-on experience with popular unit testing frameworks including JUnit for Java and Jest for JavaScript. The module covers essential testing concepts such as test cases, assertions, mocking, and test coverage analysis. Students will understand how TDD improves code quality, reduces bugs, and facilitates easier maintenance and refactoring. Through practical exercises, students will experience how writing tests first leads to better software design, clearer requirements understanding, and increased developer confidence. The module also addresses common testing anti-patterns, best practices for writing maintainable tests, and integration of testing into continuous integration pipelines. By the end of this module, students will be able to apply TDD principles to real-world projects and understand its role in modern agile development practices.
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD process of writing a failing test (Red), writing minimal code to pass (Green), and improving code structure (Refactor)
Unit Testing: Testing individual components or functions in isolation to verify they behave correctly under various conditions
Test Doubles: Objects used in place of real dependencies, including mocks, stubs, and fakes to isolate units under test
Assertions: Statements that verify expected outcomes in tests, forming the foundation of test validation
Code Coverage: Metric measuring the percentage of code executed by tests, including line, branch, and function coverage
Test Fixtures: Predefined data and object states used to ensure consistent test environments and repeatable results

title: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law
description: This module explores the fundamental relationship between changing magnetic fields and induced electric fields, focusing on Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction. Students will investigate how relative motion between conductors and magnetic fields generates electromotive force (EMF), forming the basis for understanding generators, transformers, and motors. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding through mathematical analysis and practical applications through hands-on experiments. Students will analyze magnetic flux, calculate induced EMF using Faraday's Law, and apply Lenz's Law to determine the direction of induced currents. This foundational concept bridges electrostatics and magnetostatics while introducing the dynamic interactions that power modern electrical technology. Through laboratory investigations, mathematical problem-solving, and real-world applications, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of how electromagnetic induction enables energy conversion in countless devices from power plants to electric vehicles. The module culminates with students designing and analyzing simple induction devices, demonstrating mastery of both theoretical principles and practical applications.

Faraday's Law - the induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt
Lenz's Law - the direction of induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change causing it, ensuring energy conservation
Motional EMF - EMF generated when a conductor moves through a magnetic field: ε = BLv for perpendicular motion
Self-Inductance - the property of a circuit element that opposes changes in current through induced back-EMF

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) with JavaScript
description: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing functionality. This module introduces students to the TDD cycle of Red-Green-Refactor, where developers first write failing tests (Red), implement minimal code to pass tests (Green), and then improve code quality while maintaining functionality (Refactor). Students will learn to use Jest testing framework with JavaScript to practice TDD principles on real coding problems. The module covers unit testing fundamentals, test structure and organization, mocking dependencies, and measuring test coverage. TDD is crucial for modern software development as it leads to better code design, fewer bugs, improved maintainability, and increased developer confidence when making changes. By the end of this module, students will understand how TDD transforms the development process from 'code then test' to 'test then code,' resulting in more robust and reliable software. This approach is widely adopted in agile development environments and is essential for professional software developers working in collaborative teams.

Mocking and Stubbing - Techniques for replacing dependencies with controlled test doubles to isolate code under test
Assertion Methods - Jest functions like expect(), toBe(), toEqual() used to verify expected outcomes in tests

description: This module explores the fundamental principles of wave interference and the formation of standing waves, essential concepts for understanding numerous physical phenomena from musical instruments to quantum mechanics. Students will investigate how waves combine when they meet, examining both constructive and destructive interference patterns. The module emphasizes the mathematical description of superposition and its practical applications in acoustic systems, optical devices, and electromagnetic wave behavior. Through hands-on experiments and computational modeling, students will analyze standing wave patterns in strings, air columns, and electromagnetic cavities. This knowledge forms the foundation for advanced topics including wave optics, quantum wave functions, and resonance phenomena in engineering applications. key_concepts: Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when occupying the same space, with amplitudes adding vectorially

Destructive Interference - waves cancel to produce minimum amplitude when phase difference is π, 3π, 5π, etc.
Standing Waves - stationary interference patterns formed by waves traveling in opposite directions with fixed nodes and antinodes
Resonance - enhanced amplitude oscillations occurring when driving frequency matches natural frequency of the system

title: Wave Interference and Standing Wave Patterns
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of wave interference, focusing on how waves interact when they meet in space and time. Students will investigate constructive and destructive interference patterns, analyze standing wave formation, and apply these concepts to real-world phenomena including musical instruments, architectural acoustics, and optical systems. The module emphasizes both mathematical analysis and experimental observation, bridging theoretical wave mechanics with practical applications. The module integrates mathematical modeling with laboratory skills, preparing students to analyze complex wave systems in engineering and research contexts.
key_concepts: Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when they overlap in space and time

Destructive Interference - occurs when waves are out of phase (path difference = (n+½)λ), resulting in minimum amplitude
Standing Waves - stationary wave patterns formed when identical waves traveling in opposite directions interfere
Node and Antinode - points of zero displacement (nodes) and maximum displacement (antinodes) in standing wave patterns
Phase Difference - the difference in phase between two waves, measured in radians or degrees

title: Wave-Particle Duality and the Photoelectric Effect
description: This module explores one of the most revolutionary concepts in modern physics: the dual nature of light and matter. Students will investigate how light exhibits both wave and particle characteristics through detailed examination of the photoelectric effect, a phenomenon that earned Einstein the Nobel Prize and helped establish quantum mechanics. The module begins with classical wave theory limitations, progresses through Einstein's photon hypothesis, and culminates in understanding how this duality extends to all matter via de Broglie waves. Through hands-on simulations, data analysis, and problem-solving, students will grasp how this seemingly contradictory concept resolved major physics puzzles of the early 20th century. This foundational understanding is crucial for comprehending quantum mechanics, semiconductor physics, and modern technologies like photovoltaic cells, photodiodes, and electron microscopy. The module emphasizes both historical context and practical applications, showing how abstract quantum concepts directly impact everyday technology.
key_concepts: Photoelectric Effect - emission of electrons from materials when illuminated by light above a threshold frequency, demonstrating light's particle nature
Work Function - minimum energy required to remove an electron from a material's surface, measured in electron volts (eV)
Photon Energy - quantized energy packets E = hf carried by electromagnetic radiation, where h is Planck's constant
de Broglie Wavelength - wavelength λ = h/p associated with any particle having momentum p, extending wave-particle duality to matter
Stopping Potential - minimum reverse voltage needed to prevent photoelectrons from reaching the anode in photoelectric experiments
learning_objectives: Students will analyze experimental photoelectric effect data by calculating stopping potentials, threshold frequencies, and work functions using Einstein's photoelectric equation

title: Conservation of Energy and Work-Energy Theorem
description: This module explores the fundamental principle of energy conservation and its practical applications in mechanical systems. Students will investigate how energy transforms between kinetic, potential, and other forms while remaining constant in isolated systems. The work-energy theorem serves as a bridge between force concepts and energy analysis, providing powerful problem-solving tools for complex mechanical situations. Through hands-on experiments, computational modeling, and real-world applications, students will develop intuitive understanding of energy flow in physical systems. This module emphasizes both mathematical formalism and conceptual reasoning, preparing students to analyze everything from simple pendulums to roller coasters. The content directly connects to later topics in thermodynamics, electromagnetic energy, and quantum mechanics, making it a cornerstone of physics education. Students will use energy methods to solve problems that would be difficult or impossible using force analysis alone.
key_concepts: Kinetic Energy: Energy of motion, calculated as KE = ½mv², dependent on mass and velocity squared
Potential Energy: Stored energy due to position or configuration, including gravitational (PE = mgh) and elastic (PE = ½kx²) forms
Work-Energy Theorem: Net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE)
Conservation of Mechanical Energy: Total mechanical energy remains constant when only conservative forces act
Conservative vs Non-conservative Forces: Forces like gravity conserve energy, while friction dissipates mechanical energy into heat
learning_objectives: Students will calculate kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and elastic potential energy by applying appropriate formulas to specific physical scenarios
Students will analyze energy transformations in mechanical systems through laboratory experiments with pendulums, springs, and inclined planes
Students will solve complex motion problems using conservation of energy principles and the work-energy theorem as alternatives to Newton's laws

title: Wave Interference and Superposition
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of wave interference and superposition, which govern how waves combine when they occupy the same space simultaneously. Students will investigate constructive and destructive interference patterns, analyze standing waves, and examine real-world applications including musical instruments, noise-canceling technology, and optical interference. The module emphasizes both mathematical analysis and experimental observation, bridging theoretical physics with practical applications. Through hands-on experiments with wave tanks, sound waves, and laser interference, students will develop intuitive understanding of wave behavior while mastering quantitative problem-solving techniques. This foundation is crucial for understanding advanced topics in optics, acoustics, quantum mechanics, and electromagnetic theory. The module combines visual demonstrations, mathematical modeling, and laboratory investigations to accommodate different learning styles while building essential skills in wave analysis that are fundamental to modern physics and engineering applications.
key_concepts: Superposition Principle - waves combine algebraically at each point, with total displacement equal to sum of individual wave displacements
Constructive Interference - occurs when waves meet in phase (path difference = nλ), resulting in maximum amplitude
Destructive Interference - occurs when waves meet out of phase (path difference = (n+0.5)λ), resulting in minimum amplitude
Standing Waves - stationary wave patterns formed by interference of identical waves traveling in opposite directions
Phase Difference - the relationship between wave cycles, measured in radians or degrees, determining interference type
Path Difference - the difference in distance traveled by waves from sources to observation point
learning_objectives: Students will calculate interference patterns for two-source wave systems by applying the superposition principle and path difference equations
Students will predict and verify standing wave formations through laboratory experiments with strings, air columns, and water waves
Students will analyze real-world interference phenomena using wave equations, including Young's double-slit experiment and acoustic beat frequencies
Students will design and conduct controlled experiments to measure wavelength and frequency using interference patterns and standing wave nodes

title: Newton's Laws of Motion: From Concepts to Real-World Applications
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of Newton's three laws of motion, serving as the foundation for classical mechanics and engineering applications. Students will move beyond memorizing formulas to develop deep conceptual understanding through hands-on experiments, problem-solving scenarios, and real-world case studies. The module emphasizes the interconnected nature of the laws and their universal applicability, from everyday phenomena like walking and driving to complex systems like spacecraft navigation and sports biomechanics. Through interactive demonstrations, mathematical modeling, and laboratory work, students will learn to identify forces, analyze motion, and predict outcomes in various physical systems. This understanding is crucial for advanced physics topics including energy, momentum, rotational dynamics, and serves as prerequisite knowledge for engineering disciplines. The module integrates historical context, showing how Newton's insights revolutionized our understanding of the physical world, while connecting to modern applications in technology and space exploration.
key_concepts: Newton's First Law (Inertia): Objects at rest stay at rest and objects in motion continue in uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced force
Newton's Second Law (F=ma): The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass
Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction): For every action force, there exists an equal and opposite reaction force acting on different objects

title: Wave Interference and Superposition: Understanding Constructive and Destructive Wave Interactions
description: This module explores the fundamental principle of wave superposition and its manifestations in interference phenomena. Students will investigate how waves combine when they occupy the same space, leading to constructive interference (amplitude enhancement) and destructive interference (amplitude reduction or cancellation). The module covers both one-dimensional and two-dimensional wave interference patterns, including Young's double-slit experiment, interference in water waves, and sound wave interactions. Understanding wave interference is crucial for comprehending advanced topics in optics, acoustics, quantum mechanics, and modern technologies such as noise-canceling headphones, interferometry, and holography. Students will develop both theoretical understanding through mathematical analysis and practical skills through hands-on experiments and simulations. This foundational concept bridges classical wave mechanics with quantum physics and provides essential background for understanding electromagnetic radiation, matter waves, and wave-particle duality.

Destructive Interference: Wave interaction resulting in decreased amplitude when waves are out of phase (phase difference = π, 3π, 5π, etc.)

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Fundamentals
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing functionality. TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, where developers first write a failing test (Red), then write the minimum code to make it pass (Green), and finally improve the code structure while maintaining functionality (Refactor). This approach fundamentally changes how developers think about code design, leading to better software architecture, higher code quality, and increased confidence in system reliability. Students will learn to identify testable units of code, write effective unit tests using modern testing frameworks, and understand how TDD influences software design patterns. The module emphasizes practical application through hands-on coding exercises, demonstrating how TDD reduces debugging time, improves code maintainability, and creates living documentation through comprehensive test suites. By mastering TDD principles, students develop critical thinking skills about software design and gain experience with industry-standard development practices used in agile environments.
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing failing tests first, implementing minimal code to pass, then improving code structure
Unit Testing: Creating isolated tests for individual functions or methods to verify specific behaviors and edge cases
Test Coverage: Measuring the percentage of code executed during testing to identify untested code paths and potential vulnerabilities
Mocking and Stubbing: Replacing external dependencies with controlled test doubles to isolate units under test
Assertion Patterns: Structuring tests using Arrange-Act-Assert pattern to create readable and maintainable test code
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor cycle by writing failing tests, minimal implementation code, and refactored solutions for at least three distinct programming problems
Students will analyze existing code to identify testable units and write comprehensive unit test suites through systematic decomposition of complex functions into smaller, testable components

Students will evaluate code quality improvements achieved through TDD by comparing metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, test coverage, and defect rates using industry-standard testing frameworks like Jest or JUnit
suggested_readings: Clean Code Chapter 9: Unit Tests (Martin, 2008) pp. 121-138
Test Driven Development: By Example Chapters 1-3 (Beck, 2002) pp. 1-31 - Introduction to TDD fundamentals
Journal article: The Effects of Test-Driven Development on External Quality and Productivity (Madeyski, 2010) - empirical evidence for TDD benefits
Online resource: Jest Documentation - Testing Framework Guide focusing on unit testing best practices and assertion methods

title: Linear Systems and Gaussian Elimination
description: This module introduces students to systems of linear equations and the systematic method of Gaussian elimination for solving them. Linear systems appear throughout mathematics, engineering, economics, and computer science, making this a fundamental skill for quantitative problem-solving. Students will learn to represent real-world problems as systems of linear equations, understand when systems have unique solutions, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions, and master the step-by-step process of Gaussian elimination with back-substitution. The module emphasizes both computational proficiency and conceptual understanding, helping students recognize the geometric interpretation of linear systems and connect algebraic manipulation to visual representations. By the end of this module, students will confidently solve systems involving three or more variables, interpret their solutions in context, and identify inconsistent or dependent systems. This foundation prepares students for advanced topics in linear algebra, differential equations, and optimization theory.
key_concepts: System of linear equations - a collection of two or more linear equations with the same variables that must be satisfied simultaneously
Gaussian elimination - an algorithm using elementary row operations to transform an augmented matrix into row echelon form for systematic solution
Augmented matrix - a matrix representation combining the coefficient matrix and constant vector of a linear system for efficient manipulation
Row echelon form - a matrix form where leading entries form a stair-step pattern, enabling back-substitution to find solutions
Elementary row operations - three types of matrix manipulations (row swapping, scalar multiplication, row addition) that preserve solution sets
learning_objectives: Students will solve systems of 2-4 linear equations using Gaussian elimination by performing elementary row operations systematically
Students will classify linear systems as consistent independent, consistent dependent, or inconsistent through analysis of augmented matrix row echelon forms
Students will model real-world scenarios involving multiple constraints as systems of linear equations using appropriate variable definitions and equation setup

title: Quadratic Functions: Analyzing Parabolas and Real-World Applications
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of quadratic functions, focusing on their algebraic properties, graphical representations, and practical applications. By the end of this module, students will have a solid foundation for advanced topics in algebra and calculus, while gaining confidence in applying mathematical modeling to authentic situations.
key_concepts: Standard form of quadratic function: f(x) = ax² + bx + c, where a ≠ 0 determines the parabola's width and direction
Vertex form: f(x) = a(x-h)² + k, where (h,k) represents the parabola's vertex and provides direct access to maximum/minimum values
Discriminant: b² - 4ac determines the nature and number of real roots (positive = two real roots, zero = one repeated root, negative = no real roots)
Axis of symmetry: the vertical line x = -b/(2a) that divides the parabola into two mirror-image halves
Completing the square: algebraic technique for converting standard form to vertex form by creating perfect square trinomials
learning_objectives: Students will convert quadratic functions between standard form (ax² + bx + c), vertex form (a(x-h)² + k), and factored form (a(x-p)(x-q)) by applying algebraic manipulation techniques

Students will analyze and graph parabolas by identifying the vertex, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, y-intercept, and direction of opening through systematic coordinate plotting and formula application

description: This module focuses on understanding and implementing fundamental shortest path algorithms, which are essential for solving routing, navigation, and network optimization problems in computer science. key_concepts: Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a source vertex to all other vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edges

key_concepts: Graph representation (adjacency matrix vs adjacency list) - different methods for storing graph data structures with their respective memory and access time implications

title: Limits and Continuity: Building the Foundation of Calculus
description: This module introduces the fundamental concept of limits, which forms the cornerstone of differential and integral calculus. Students will explore the intuitive notion of approaching a value without necessarily reaching it, then formalize this understanding through epsilon-delta definitions and limit laws. The concept of continuity emerges naturally from limits, providing the mathematical framework for understanding smooth functions and their behaviors. Through graphical analysis, algebraic manipulation, and real-world applications, students will master techniques for evaluating limits of various function types, including rational functions, trigonometric functions, and piecewise functions. Special attention is given to indeterminate forms and L'Hôpital's rule as powerful problem-solving tools. Understanding limits is crucial for success in calculus, as derivatives and integrals are defined as specific types of limits. This module bridges the gap between precalculus algebra and advanced calculus concepts, establishing the rigorous mathematical thinking required for higher-level mathematics courses.
key_concepts: One-sided limits: The behavior of a function as the input approaches a specific value from either the left or right side exclusively
Epsilon-delta definition: The formal mathematical definition of a limit using arbitrary small positive numbers to establish precise bounds
Continuity types: Classification of function behavior including removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and infinite discontinuities
Indeterminate forms: Expressions like 0/0 or ∞/∞ that require special techniques such as L'Hôpital's rule or algebraic manipulation to evaluate
Squeeze theorem: A method for finding limits by trapping a function between two other functions with known limits
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate limits of functions using algebraic techniques, graphical analysis, and limit laws by solving progressively complex limit problems involving rational, trigonometric, and exponential functions
Students will determine continuity of functions at specific points and over intervals through systematic application of the three-part continuity definition and identification of discontinuity types
Students will apply L'Hôpital's rule to resolve indeterminate forms using appropriate differentiation techniques and recognize when the rule applies versus alternative methods

title: Advanced Binary Trees: AVL Trees and Balancing Algorithms
description: This module introduces students to self-balancing binary search trees, specifically AVL trees, which maintain logarithmic time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion operations. Students will understand the fundamental problem of tree degeneration in basic binary search trees and learn how automatic balancing mechanisms solve this critical issue. The module covers rotation algorithms (single and double rotations), balance factor calculations, and the mathematical principles behind AVL tree height guarantees. Through hands-on implementation and analysis, students will gain practical experience with one of the most important data structures in computer science, used extensively in database indexing, memory management, and efficient algorithm design. This knowledge forms the foundation for understanding other self-balancing trees like Red-Black trees and provides crucial insights into algorithm optimization and performance analysis.
key_concepts: Balance Factor: Integer value (-1, 0, +1) representing height difference between left and right subtrees
Single Rotation: Fundamental restructuring operation that corrects simple imbalances through one pivot movement
Double Rotation: Complex balancing operation combining two single rotations to fix inside-heavy imbalances
Height Invariant: Mathematical property ensuring AVL tree height never exceeds 1.44 * log(n+2) for optimal performance
learning_objectives: Students will implement complete AVL tree insertion and deletion algorithms by coding rotation functions and balance factor maintenance

title: Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval
description: This module explores hash tables, one of the most fundamental and widely-used data structures in computer science. Hash tables provide average-case O(1) time complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, making them essential for applications requiring fast data access. Students will learn how hash functions transform keys into array indices, understand different collision resolution strategies, and analyze the trade-offs between time and space complexity. The module covers practical implementations in various programming languages and examines real-world applications including database indexing, caching systems, and compiler symbol tables. Students will gain hands-on experience implementing hash tables from scratch, comparing different hash functions, and optimizing performance through load factor management. This knowledge is crucial for software engineering interviews, system design, and building efficient algorithms. The module also addresses security considerations in hash function design and introduces cryptographic hash functions used in blockchain and data integrity verification.
key_concepts: Hash Function: A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (hash codes) used as array indices
Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle when multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
Load Factor: The ratio of filled slots to total slots in a hash table, affecting performance and memory usage
Universal Hashing: A randomized approach to hash function selection that provides theoretical guarantees on average-case performance
Perfect Hashing: Hash functions that produce no collisions for a specific set of keys, used in static datasets
learning_objectives: Students will implement a hash table data structure with chaining collision resolution by writing complete code in Python or Java
Students will analyze hash function quality and distribution through experimental measurement of collision rates and clustering

Students will design optimal hash table configurations by calculating appropriate load factors and table sizes for specific use cases
