The module emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical implementation, connecting mathematical concepts like load factor and uniform distribution to concrete programming challenges.
key_concepts: Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly
Collision Resolution - Techniques like chaining (linked lists) or open addressing (probing) used when multiple keys hash to the same index
Load Factor - The ratio of stored elements to table size that affects performance and determines when to resize the hash table
learning_objectives: Students will implement a hash table with chaining collision resolution by writing complete Java or Python code with insert, delete, and search methods
Students will analyze hash function quality through calculating collision rates and load factors using provided datasets
Students will compare collision resolution strategies using empirical testing of linear probing, quadratic probing, and separate chaining implementations
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 11 - Hash Tables (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 253-285
Journal article: Universal Hashing and Perfect Hashing (Carter & Wegman, 1979) - focus on theoretical foundations
Online resource: GeeksforGeeks Hash Table tutorials - collision resolution implementation examples and visualization tools

title: Graph Algorithms: Depth-First Search and Breadth-First Search
description: This module introduces students to fundamental graph traversal algorithms that form the backbone of many computer science applications. Graph algorithms are essential for solving problems in network analysis, social media platforms, GPS navigation systems, web crawling, and artificial intelligence pathfinding. Students will learn to implement and analyze Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithms, understanding their distinct approaches to exploring graph structures. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, covering time and space complexity analysis, algorithm design patterns, and real-world applications. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithm visualization, students will develop intuition for when to apply each traversal method. This foundational knowledge prepares students for advanced topics like shortest path algorithms, minimum spanning trees, and graph-based machine learning techniques. The module bridges abstract mathematical concepts with concrete programming skills, demonstrating how theoretical computer science directly translates to practical problem-solving tools used in modern software development.
key_concepts: Depth-First Search (DFS) - A graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack data structure (explicit or recursive call stack)
Breadth-First Search (BFS) - A graph traversal algorithm that explores all vertices at the current depth level before moving to vertices at the next depth level, using a queue data structure
Graph representations - Methods for storing graph data including adjacency lists (space-efficient for sparse graphs) and adjacency matrices (constant-time edge lookup)
Traversal tree - The tree structure formed by the edges used during graph traversal, which differs from the original graph and depends on the starting vertex and algorithm choice
Connected components - Maximal sets of vertices in an undirected graph where each vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the same component
learning_objectives: Students will implement both DFS and BFS algorithms in Python by writing complete functions that traverse adjacency list and adjacency matrix representations
Students will analyze time and space complexity of graph traversal algorithms through big-O notation calculations and empirical testing on graphs of varying sizes
Students will solve real-world problems using DFS and BFS by applying appropriate traversal methods to scenarios like maze solving, connected components detection, and shortest path finding
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 22 Elementary Graph Algorithms (Cormen et al., 2009) pp. 594-630
Journal article: A Comparison of Graph Traversal Algorithms (Kumar & Patel, 2019) - focus on practical performance analysis
GeeksforGeeks: Graph Data Structure and Algorithms - interactive examples and code implementations
Visualgo.net: Graph Traversal section - animated algorithm demonstrations and step-by-step execution

title: Graph Algorithms and Network Analysis
description: This module introduces fundamental graph algorithms and their applications in network analysis, providing students with essential skills for solving complex computational problems involving relationships and connections. Graph theory serves as the mathematical foundation for understanding networks in social media, transportation systems, computer networks, and biological systems. Students will explore core algorithms including breadth-first search, depth-first search, shortest path algorithms, and minimum spanning trees. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation, connecting abstract mathematical concepts to real-world applications. Through hands-on programming exercises, students will implement these algorithms and analyze their time and space complexity. The module also covers graph representation techniques and how algorithm choice impacts performance with different data structures. By the end of this module, students will possess the analytical skills to identify graph-based problems in various domains and select appropriate algorithms for efficient solutions. This foundation is crucial for advanced topics in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and distributed systems, making it an essential component of computer science education.
key_concepts: Graph Representation - Methods for storing graphs in memory including adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and edge lists with trade-offs analysis
Graph Traversal - Systematic exploration techniques including BFS for shortest unweighted paths and DFS for topological sorting and cycle detection
Shortest Path Algorithms - Dijkstra's algorithm for non-negative weights and Bellman-Ford for graphs with negative edges, including path reconstruction
Minimum Spanning Trees - Algorithms to find the lowest-cost subgraph that connects all vertices, crucial for network design optimization
Topological Sorting - Ordering vertices in directed acyclic graphs to represent dependencies and prerequisite relationships
learning_objectives: Students will implement breadth-first search and depth-first search algorithms by coding solutions in Python for graph traversal problems
Students will analyze shortest path problems through hands-on application of Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford algorithms on weighted graphs
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency using Big O notation to compare time and space complexity of different graph algorithms
Students will design solutions for network connectivity problems by applying minimum spanning tree algorithms including Kruskal's and Prim's methods
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 22-24 Graph Algorithms (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 589-677
Journal article: Efficient Graph Algorithms for Network Analysis (Johnson, 2023) - focus on practical implementation strategies
Online resource: GeeksforGeeks Graph Algorithms Section - interactive examples and complexity analysis
Research paper: Applications of Graph Theory in Social Network Analysis (Smith & Chen, 2023) - real-world case studies

title: Simple Harmonic Motion: Springs, Pendulums, and Oscillations
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of simple harmonic motion (SHM), one of the most important concepts in physics that appears across multiple disciplines from mechanical engineering to quantum mechanics. Students will investigate how objects oscillate about equilibrium positions, focusing on mass-spring systems and simple pendulums as primary examples. The module emphasizes both mathematical modeling and experimental observation, helping students understand how restoring forces create predictable, sinusoidal motion patterns. Through hands-on experiments and computational analysis, students will discover the relationships between period, frequency, amplitude, and energy in oscillating systems. This foundational knowledge is essential for understanding wave motion, AC circuits, molecular vibrations, and many other phenomena in advanced physics courses. The module bridges theoretical physics with practical applications, showing how SHM principles apply to everything from car suspension systems to atomic vibrations in crystalline structures.
key_concepts: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium (F = -kx)
Period (T) and Frequency (f) - time for one complete oscillation and number of oscillations per unit time, related by f = 1/T
Angular frequency (ω) - rate of change of phase angle in oscillation, related to period by ω = 2π/T = √(k/m) for springs
Amplitude (A) - maximum displacement from equilibrium position, determines total mechanical energy of the system
Phase constant (φ) - determines initial conditions of motion at t = 0, affecting starting position and velocity
Restoring force - force that acts to return oscillating object to equilibrium position, always directed opposite to displacement
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the mathematical relationships in simple harmonic motion by deriving and applying the equations x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), v(t) = -Aω sin(ωt + φ), and a(t) = -Aω² cos(ωt + φ)
Students will measure and predict oscillation periods through laboratory experiments with mass-spring systems and simple pendulums using data collection software and statistical analysis
Students will evaluate energy transformations in oscillating systems using conservation of energy principles to calculate kinetic and potential energy at different positions during oscillation
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 14: Periodic Motion (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 439-472
Journal article: Teaching Simple Harmonic Motion with Real-World Applications (Physics Education, 2019) - focus on pedagogical approaches and common misconceptions
Online resource: PhET Simulations - Masses and Springs interactive simulation for visualization of SHM parameters
Video lectures: MIT 8.01 Physics I Lecture 10 - Hooke's Law, Simple Harmonic Motion (30 minutes)

title: Derivatives and Rate of Change in Calculus I
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental concept of derivatives as the instantaneous rate of change of a function. Building from the geometric interpretation of slopes of tangent lines, students will develop both conceptual understanding and computational fluency with derivative rules. The module emphasizes the connection between limits and derivatives, establishing the derivative as the limit of difference quotients. Students will explore real-world applications including velocity, acceleration, population growth, and optimization problems. Through graphical analysis, algebraic manipulation, and practical problem-solving, students will master the power rule, product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule. This foundation is critical for advanced calculus topics and applications across physics, engineering, economics, and biological sciences. The module balances theoretical understanding with computational skills, preparing students to model dynamic systems and solve rate-related problems in their academic and professional pursuits.
key_concepts: Derivative as a limit: The formal definition f'(x) = lim[h→0] (f(x+h) - f(x))/h
Differentiation rules: Power rule (d/dx[x^n] = nx^(n-1)), product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule for composite functions
Rate of change applications: Velocity as derivative of position, marginal cost in economics, and related rates problems
learning_objectives: Students will compute derivatives of polynomial, exponential, and trigonometric functions by applying differentiation rules including power, product, quotient, and chain rules
Students will interpret derivatives as instantaneous rates of change through graphical analysis and real-world problem contexts
Students will solve applied rate problems using derivative concepts in physics, economics, and optimization scenarios
suggested_readings: Calculus: Early Transcendentals Chapter 3: Derivatives (Stewart, 2020) pp. 147-220
Journal article: The Derivative Concept and Student Difficulties (Orton, 1983) - focus on common misconceptions
Online resource: Khan Academy Calculus - Derivative Introduction and Rules modules with interactive exercises

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Uncovering Patterns and Anomalies
description: This module focuses on the critical first phase of any data analysis project: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). Students will learn systematic approaches to examine datasets, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses before formal statistical modeling. EDA serves as the foundation for all subsequent analysis, helping analysts understand data structure, quality issues, and underlying relationships. Through hands-on practice with real datasets, students will master both univariate and multivariate exploration techniques using statistical summaries, visualizations, and correlation analysis. The module emphasizes the iterative nature of EDA, where initial findings guide deeper investigation. Students will learn to balance automated discovery tools with manual investigation, developing intuition for when patterns are meaningful versus coincidental. This foundational skill set is essential across all data analysis domains, from business intelligence to scientific research, making it crucial for building analytical thinking and practical data manipulation skills.
key_concepts: Univariate Analysis: Examining single variables through measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape to understand individual variable characteristics
Outlier Detection: Systematic identification of data points that deviate significantly from expected patterns using statistical methods like Z-scores and boxplot analysis
Correlation vs. Causation: Understanding the difference between statistical relationships and causal relationships, including spurious correlations and confounding variables
Data Quality Assessment: Evaluating completeness, consistency, accuracy, and validity of datasets through missing value analysis and data type verification
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive univariate analysis by calculating descriptive statistics, creating distribution plots, and identifying outliers using the interquartile range method
Students will discover multivariate relationships through correlation matrices, scatterplot matrices, and categorical association tests using chi-square analysis
Students will synthesize EDA findings using Python/R to create professional data profiling reports that include data quality assessments and actionable insights
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' from Python for Data Analysis (McKinney, 2022) pp. 245-289
Journal article: 'Exploratory Data Analysis: A Practical Guide' (Tukey Revisited, 2021) - focus on modern EDA workflows and best practices
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA Course - hands-on exercises with interactive notebooks and real datasets

title: Exploratory Data Analysis with Python: Unveiling Data Stories Through Visualization and Statistics
description: This module introduces students to the critical first phase of any data analysis project: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). EDA is the detective work of data science, where analysts examine datasets to understand their structure, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses before applying formal modeling techniques. Students will learn to approach unfamiliar datasets systematically, using Python's powerful libraries including pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, and scipy to extract meaningful insights. The module emphasizes both statistical rigor and visual storytelling, teaching students to create compelling data narratives that inform business decisions. Through hands-on analysis of real-world datasets from domains like e-commerce, healthcare, and social media, students will develop the intuition to ask the right questions of their data. This foundational skill set is essential for data analysts, as proper EDA often reveals insights that sophisticated machine learning models might miss, while also preventing costly errors in downstream analysis.
key_concepts: Data profiling - systematic examination of dataset structure, completeness, and quality metrics
Statistical summaries - central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape measures for numerical and categorical variables
Correlation analysis - measuring and interpreting linear and non-linear relationships between variables
Outlier detection - identifying anomalous data points using statistical methods (IQR, z-scores) and visual inspection
Data visualization principles - selecting appropriate chart types and design elements to effectively communicate findings
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive dataset profiling by implementing systematic data quality checks, missing value analysis, and distribution assessments using pandas and numpy
Students will identify meaningful patterns and relationships through creating and interpreting correlation matrices, scatter plots, box plots, and statistical summary tables
Students will communicate data insights using advanced visualization techniques in matplotlib and seaborn to create publication-ready charts, dashboards, and statistical plots
suggested_readings: Python for Data Analysis: Chapter 9 'Plotting and Visualization' (McKinney, 2022) pp. 267-312
Journal article: 'Exploratory Data Analysis: A Practical Guide for Data Scientists' (Tukey Foundation, 2021) - focus on statistical validation techniques
Online resource: Kaggle Learn - 'Data Visualization' course modules 1-4 covering seaborn fundamentals
Case study: 'Customer Segmentation Analysis: An EDA Approach' (Harvard Business Analytics, 2023) - real-world application examples

title: Wave Interference and Diffraction Phenomena
description: This module explores the fundamental wave behaviors of interference and diffraction, critical phenomena that occur when waves encounter obstacles or interact with each other. Students will investigate constructive and destructive interference patterns, analyze single-slit and double-slit diffraction, and examine practical applications including noise-canceling technology, optical instruments, and wireless communication systems. Through hands-on experiments with laser light, sound waves, and water ripples, students will develop both conceptual understanding and mathematical proficiency in predicting wave behavior. The module bridges classical wave theory with modern applications, demonstrating how these principles underpin technologies from microscopy to radio astronomy. Students will use simulation software to visualize complex wave interactions and conduct laboratory investigations to measure wavelengths and interference patterns. This foundation is essential for understanding advanced topics in optics, quantum mechanics, and electromagnetic wave propagation.
key_concepts: Constructive interference - waves combining in phase to produce maximum amplitude when path difference equals integer multiples of wavelength
Destructive interference - waves combining out of phase to produce minimum amplitude when path difference equals odd multiples of half-wavelength
Diffraction - wave bending around obstacles or through apertures, with angular spread inversely proportional to aperture size relative to wavelength
Coherence - degree of correlation between wave phases, essential for observable interference patterns in both temporal and spatial domains
Path difference - geometric difference in distances traveled by waves from sources to observation point, determining interference condition
learning_objectives: Students will calculate path differences and predict interference patterns by applying the principles of constructive and destructive interference to double-slit and multiple-slit configurations
Students will analyze single-slit diffraction patterns through laboratory experiments measuring intensity distributions and comparing results to theoretical predictions
Students will evaluate real-world applications of wave interference using mathematical models to explain phenomena in acoustics, optics, and electromagnetic wave systems
suggested_readings: University Physics: Chapter 35 'Interference' and Chapter 36 'Diffraction' (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 1162-1243
Journal article: 'Visualizing wave interference patterns in undergraduate physics education' (American Journal of Physics, 2019) - pedagogical approaches to teaching interference
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - 'Wave Interference' and 'Single Slit Diffraction' modules with guided exploration activities

title: Simple Harmonic Motion and Oscillations
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of simple harmonic motion (SHM), one of the most fundamental concepts in physics that appears across multiple disciplines from mechanical systems to quantum mechanics. Students will investigate the mathematical framework governing oscillatory motion, analyze real-world examples ranging from pendulums to molecular vibrations, and develop problem-solving skills essential for advanced physics courses. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical applications, connecting abstract mathematical concepts to observable phenomena. Through hands-on experiments, computational modeling, and analytical problem-solving, students will master the relationship between force, displacement, velocity, and acceleration in oscillatory systems. This foundational knowledge serves as a gateway to understanding wave mechanics, resonance phenomena, and energy conservation principles that are crucial in fields such as engineering, acoustics, seismology, and quantum physics. The module also develops critical thinking skills by requiring students to predict system behavior, analyze experimental data, and explain discrepancies between theoretical models and real-world observations.
key_concepts: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium position
Angular frequency (ω) - measure of how rapidly oscillation occurs, related to period by ω = 2π/T
Phase constant (φ) - determines initial conditions of oscillatory motion at t = 0
Damping - energy loss mechanism that causes amplitude to decrease over time in real oscillators
Resonance - phenomenon where driving frequency matches natural frequency, causing maximum amplitude response
learning_objectives: Students will derive and apply the equations of motion for simple harmonic oscillators by analyzing the relationship between restoring force and displacement using calculus-based methods
Students will predict and measure the period and frequency of various oscillating systems through laboratory experiments involving pendulums, springs, and mass-spring systems
Students will analyze energy transformations in oscillatory motion using graphical analysis and computational simulations to visualize kinetic and potential energy variations
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 15: Oscillations (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 458-495
Journal article: The Physics of Oscillations in Biological Systems (Goldbeter, 2018) - focus on mathematical modeling applications
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Masses and Springs simulation with guided worksheet
Supplementary reading: Classical Dynamics Chapter 3 (Taylor, 2005) pp. 68-89 - advanced mathematical treatment

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Pattern Discovery and Visual Investigation
description: This module focuses on the critical first phase of data analysis where analysts systematically explore datasets to uncover patterns, anomalies, and relationships before formal hypothesis testing or modeling. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) serves as the foundation for all subsequent analytical work, helping analysts understand data structure, identify quality issues, and generate informed hypotheses. Students will master both statistical and visual techniques for data exploration, learning to ask the right questions of their data and communicate findings effectively. The module emphasizes practical application using real-world datasets from business, healthcare, and social sciences. By combining descriptive statistics, data visualization principles, and systematic investigation techniques, students develop the analytical intuition necessary for advanced data science work. This hands-on approach ensures students can immediately apply EDA techniques to identify outliers, understand distributions, detect correlations, and prepare data for modeling. The skills developed here are essential for any data professional, as EDA directly impacts the quality and validity of all downstream analytical work.
key_concepts: Univariate Analysis: Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
Data Profiling: Systematic assessment of data quality, completeness, and structure to identify missing values, duplicates, and inconsistencies
Correlation vs Causation: Understanding the distinction between statistical relationships and causal mechanisms in data interpretation
Distribution Analysis: Identifying and interpreting normal, skewed, and multimodal distributions using visual and statistical tests
Outlier Detection: Methods for identifying and handling extreme values using IQR, z-scores, and visualization techniques
learning_objectives: Students will systematically explore datasets to identify patterns, outliers, and data quality issues by applying univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analysis techniques
Students will create compelling data visualizations that reveal insights and support decision-making through the strategic use of histograms, scatter plots, box plots, and correlation matrices
Students will formulate data-driven hypotheses and research questions using Python libraries (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn) and statistical summary techniques

title: Conservation of Energy in Mechanical Systems
description: This module explores the fundamental principle of energy conservation in mechanical systems, focusing on the interplay between kinetic energy, potential energy, and work. Students will develop a deep understanding of how energy transforms between different forms while remaining constant in isolated systems. The module emphasizes problem-solving strategies for real-world applications including projectile motion, pendulums, roller coasters, and collision scenarios. Through hands-on experiments and computational modeling, students will discover how energy conservation serves as a powerful analytical tool that often provides simpler solutions than force-based approaches. This foundational concept bridges introductory mechanics with advanced topics in thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and quantum physics. Students will learn to identify when energy methods are most appropriate and develop intuition for energy flow in complex systems. The module includes extensive practice with energy bar charts, graphical analysis, and mathematical derivations that prepare students for advanced physics coursework and engineering applications.
key_concepts: Kinetic Energy (KE = ½mv²) - energy of motion depending on mass and velocity squared
Gravitational Potential Energy (PE = mgh) - stored energy based on position in gravitational field
Elastic Potential Energy (PE = ½kx²) - energy stored in deformed springs and elastic materials
Work-Energy Theorem - net work done on object equals change in kinetic energy
Conservation of Mechanical Energy - total mechanical energy remains constant in absence of non-conservative forces
Non-conservative Forces - forces like friction that convert mechanical energy to thermal energy
learning_objectives: Students will calculate kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and elastic potential energy by applying the appropriate formulas and identifying relevant variables in given scenarios
Students will analyze energy transformations in mechanical systems through constructing and interpreting energy bar charts for multi-step motion problems
Students will solve complex motion problems using the work-energy theorem and conservation of mechanical energy principles instead of kinematic equations
Students will predict system behavior in non-conservative systems by accounting for energy dissipation due to friction and air resistance
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 7: Potential Energy and Energy Conservation (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 209-245
Journal article: Energy Methods in Introductory Physics (Henderson, 2019) - pedagogical approaches to energy problem-solving
PhET Simulations: Energy Skate Park and Pendulum Lab - interactive energy visualization tools
Khan Academy: Work and Energy unit - video lectures on energy conservation applications

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Uncovering Patterns Through Statistical Investigation
description: This module focuses on Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), a critical phase in the data analysis process where analysts systematically examine datasets to understand their structure, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses before formal modeling. EDA serves as the foundation for all subsequent analytical work, enabling data scientists to make informed decisions about data cleaning, feature selection, and analytical approaches. Students will learn to combine statistical techniques with data visualization to extract meaningful insights from raw data. The module emphasizes hands-on practice with real-world datasets, teaching students to think critically about data quality, distribution patterns, and relationships between variables. Through systematic exploration techniques, students will develop the analytical mindset necessary to approach unfamiliar datasets confidently. This module bridges the gap between data collection and advanced analytics, providing essential skills for identifying data issues early, understanding variable relationships, and communicating preliminary findings to stakeholders. Mastery of EDA techniques is crucial for preventing costly analytical errors and ensuring robust, reliable results in any data-driven project.
key_concepts: Univariate Analysis: Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
Bivariate Analysis: Investigation of relationships between two variables using correlation coefficients, cross-tabulation, and comparative visualizations
Data Quality Assessment: Systematic evaluation of completeness, consistency, accuracy, and validity of dataset elements
Outlier Detection: Methods for identifying unusual data points including statistical tests (Z-score, IQR) and visualization techniques
Distribution Analysis: Examination of data patterns including normality testing, skewness assessment, and distribution fitting
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive univariate and bivariate analyses by applying descriptive statistics, distribution assessment techniques, and correlation analysis to identify key dataset characteristics
Students will create effective data visualizations through hands-on practice with histograms, box plots, scatter plots, and heatmaps to communicate data patterns and anomalies
Students will detect and evaluate outliers, missing data patterns, and data quality issues using statistical tests, visualization techniques, and domain knowledge validation

title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy in Real-World Systems
description: This module explores the fundamental principle of energy conservation, focusing specifically on mechanical energy in both idealized and real-world scenarios. Students will investigate how kinetic and potential energy transform into one another while examining the role of non-conservative forces like friction and air resistance. Through hands-on experiments, computational modeling, and practical applications, learners will develop a deep understanding of energy conservation principles that govern everything from roller coasters to planetary motion. The module emphasizes problem-solving strategies for complex systems and connects theoretical concepts to engineering applications, renewable energy systems, and everyday phenomena. Students will use both analytical methods and digital tools to analyze energy transformations, preparing them for advanced physics topics while developing critical thinking skills about energy efficiency and sustainability in modern technology.
key_concepts: Mechanical Energy: The sum of kinetic and potential energy in a system, representing the total energy available for motion and position
Conservative Forces: Forces like gravity and spring forces where work done is path-independent and energy can be fully recovered
Non-conservative Forces: Forces like friction and air resistance that dissipate mechanical energy into thermal energy, making energy transformations irreversible
Energy Diagrams: Graphical representations showing potential energy as a function of position, used to predict motion and identify equilibrium points
Work-Energy Theorem: The relationship between net work done on an object and its change in kinetic energy
learning_objectives: Students will calculate kinetic and potential energy transformations by analyzing motion in gravitational, elastic, and electromagnetic fields using conservation principles
Students will predict system behavior in the presence of non-conservative forces through experimental data collection and computational modeling
Students will evaluate energy efficiency in real-world applications using energy conservation analysis and identify optimization strategies for mechanical systems
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 8: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 235-275
Journal article: Energy Analysis of Mechanical Systems in Engineering Applications (Martinez et al., 2019) - focus on sections 2-4 covering real-world energy losses
Online resource: PhET Energy Skate Park Simulation - interactive exploration of energy conservation with adjustable friction and track design
Case study: Renewable Energy Systems and Energy Storage (MIT OpenCourseWare) - mechanical energy applications in wind and hydroelectric power

title: Simple Harmonic Motion and Oscillatory Systems
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of simple harmonic motion (SHM) and oscillatory systems, which form the foundation for understanding waves, resonance, and periodic phenomena throughout physics and engineering. Students will investigate the mathematical relationships governing oscillating systems, from mass-spring systems to pendulums, and discover how these principles apply to real-world applications including musical instruments, building design, and mechanical systems. Through hands-on experiments and computational modeling, students will develop both theoretical understanding and practical problem-solving skills. The module emphasizes the connection between energy conservation, restoring forces, and periodic motion, while introducing key mathematical tools including differential equations and trigonometric functions in physical contexts. By examining oscillatory motion at both macroscopic and microscopic scales, students will prepare for advanced topics in waves, quantum mechanics, and thermodynamics. This foundation is essential for understanding phenomena ranging from atomic vibrations in solids to the behavior of electrical circuits and mechanical engineering systems.
key_concepts: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) - periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium position
Angular frequency (ω) - measure of how rapidly oscillation occurs, related to period T by ω = 2π/T
Damped oscillations - oscillatory motion with amplitude decreasing over time due to energy dissipation
Resonance - phenomenon where driving frequency matches natural frequency, causing maximum amplitude response
Phase relationships - time-dependent relationships between position, velocity, and acceleration in oscillatory motion
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the motion of oscillating systems by applying Newton's laws and solving the simple harmonic motion differential equation to predict position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time
Students will determine system parameters (frequency, period, amplitude, phase) through experimental data collection and analysis using pendulums, mass-spring systems, and computer simulations
Students will evaluate energy transformations in oscillatory systems using conservation principles to solve complex problems involving damping, driving forces, and resonance phenomena

title: Statistical Hypothesis Testing for Data-Driven Decision Making
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical applications of statistical hypothesis testing in data analysis. Students will learn to formulate research questions as testable hypotheses, select appropriate statistical tests based on data characteristics, and interpret results to make informed business and research decisions. The module emphasizes hands-on application using real-world datasets, covering parametric tests (t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square) and their non-parametric alternatives. Students will master the critical thinking skills needed to avoid common statistical pitfalls, understand p-values and confidence intervals, and communicate findings effectively to non-technical stakeholders. By the end of this module, students will confidently conduct hypothesis tests using statistical software and understand when and why different tests are appropriate for various data scenarios.
key_concepts: Null and Alternative Hypotheses - formal statements that define what the statistical test will evaluate
P-values and Statistical Significance - probability of observing results as extreme as those found, assuming null hypothesis is true
Type I and Type II Errors - false positive (rejecting true null) and false negative (accepting false null) error rates
Effect Size and Practical Significance - magnitude of difference or relationship beyond statistical significance
Parametric vs Non-parametric Tests - tests assuming normal distribution vs distribution-free alternatives
learning_objectives: Students will formulate null and alternative hypotheses for business and research questions by analyzing problem statements and identifying key variables
Students will execute appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, Mann-Whitney U) through hands-on practice with Python/R statistical libraries
Students will interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes using real datasets to make data-driven recommendations
Students will evaluate test assumptions and select between parametric and non-parametric alternatives by examining data distributions and sample characteristics
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Hypothesis Testing Fundamentals' in Statistics for Business Analytics (Anderson et al., 2020) pp. 284-342
Journal article: 'The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose' (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) - understanding p-value interpretation
Online resource: Kaggle Learn - 'Statistical Tests in Python' interactive tutorials with datasets
Case study: 'A/B Testing at Netflix' (Harvard Business Review, 2019) - real-world hypothesis testing application

title: API Design and Implementation with RESTful Services
description: This module provides comprehensive coverage of designing, building, and consuming RESTful APIs - a critical skill for modern software development. Students will learn the principles of REST architecture, HTTP methods, status codes, and resource modeling while gaining hands-on experience building production-ready APIs. The module emphasizes practical implementation using industry-standard tools and frameworks, teaching students how to create well-documented, secure, and scalable web services. Through real-world scenarios, students will understand how APIs serve as the backbone of distributed systems, mobile applications, and microservices architectures. By the end of this module, students will be equipped to design APIs that follow industry best practices, implement proper error handling and authentication, and create comprehensive documentation that enables seamless integration by other developers and systems.
key_concepts: REST Architecture - Representational State Transfer principles including statelessness, uniform interface, and client-server separation
HTTP Methods and Status Codes - Proper use of GET, POST, PUT, DELETE methods and meaningful status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 500)
Resource Modeling - Designing URL structures and data representations that logically map to business entities and operations
API Versioning - Strategies for maintaining backward compatibility while evolving API functionality over time
Authentication and Authorization - Implementing JWT tokens, OAuth, and API key-based security mechanisms
learning_objectives: Students will design RESTful API endpoints following industry standards by applying HTTP methods, status codes, and resource naming conventions
Students will implement a complete REST API through hands-on coding exercises using Node.js/Express or Python/Flask framework

title: Electric Circuits and Ohm's Law: Fundamentals of Current, Voltage, and Resistance
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental principles governing electric circuits, with a focus on understanding the relationships between current, voltage, and resistance through Ohm's Law. Students will explore how electric charge flows through conductors, learn to analyze simple circuits using mathematical relationships, and develop practical skills in circuit construction and measurement. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and hands-on application, preparing students to solve real-world electrical problems. Through laboratory experiments and problem-solving exercises, students will gain confidence in using multimeters, constructing circuits on breadboards, and predicting circuit behavior. This foundation is essential for advanced topics in electromagnetism, electronics, and electrical engineering applications.
key_concepts: Electric Current (I) - the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A)
Voltage (V) - the electric potential difference that drives current through a circuit, measured in volts (V)
Resistance (R) - the opposition to current flow in a material, measured in ohms (Ω)
Ohm's Law - the fundamental relationship V = IR connecting voltage, current, and resistance
Series Circuits - circuits where components are connected end-to-end in a single current path
Parallel Circuits - circuits where components are connected across common points, creating multiple current paths
Power Dissipation - the rate of energy conversion in electrical components, calculated as P = VI
learning_objectives: Students will calculate current, voltage, and resistance in series and parallel circuits by applying Ohm's Law and Kirchhoff's rules to solve quantitative problems
Students will measure electrical quantities in physical circuits through hands-on laboratory experiments using multimeters and breadboards
Students will analyze circuit diagrams and predict circuit behavior using schematic reading skills and mathematical modeling techniques
Students will construct functional electric circuits by following schematic diagrams and troubleshooting common circuit problems
suggested_readings: Physics textbook chapter: Electric Circuits (Serway & Jewett, 2018) pp. 756-789
Journal article: Teaching Ohm's Law through Interactive Simulations (Physics Education, 2019) - pedagogical approaches
Online resource: PhET Circuit Construction Kit - interactive circuit simulation exercises
Laboratory manual: DC Circuits Lab Guide (Local Institution) - experimental procedures and safety protocols

title: API Design and Integration Patterns
description: This module focuses on designing, building, and integrating Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) following industry best practices and established patterns. Students will learn to create RESTful APIs, implement proper authentication and authorization mechanisms, handle error scenarios gracefully, and integrate third-party services effectively. The module emphasizes practical skills including API documentation, versioning strategies, rate limiting, and security considerations. Through hands-on projects, students will build production-ready APIs and consume external services while understanding the architectural decisions that impact scalability, maintainability, and user experience. This module is essential for modern software development as APIs serve as the backbone of distributed systems, microservices architectures, and mobile applications. Students will gain expertise in tools and frameworks commonly used in the industry, preparing them for real-world development scenarios where seamless integration between systems is critical for business success.
key_concepts: REST architectural principles - Representational State Transfer constraints including statelessness, uniform interface, and resource-based URLs
API authentication patterns - Methods for securing APIs including JWT (JSON Web Tokens), OAuth 2.0 flows, and API key management strategies
Error handling and status codes - HTTP status code semantics, structured error responses, and graceful failure mechanisms
Rate limiting and throttling - Techniques for controlling API usage including token bucket, sliding window, and fixed window algorithms
API versioning strategies - Approaches to evolving APIs including URL versioning, header versioning, and backward compatibility maintenance
learning_objectives: Students will design and implement RESTful APIs following OpenAPI specification standards by creating endpoints with proper HTTP methods, status codes, and resource modeling
Students will implement secure API authentication and authorization mechanisms through hands-on development using JWT tokens, OAuth 2.0, and API key management
Students will integrate third-party APIs and handle error scenarios using industry-standard libraries and implementing retry logic, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation patterns
suggested_readings: RESTful Web APIs: Services for a Changing World (Richardson & Amundsen, 2013) pp. 45-89, 156-201
Journal article: API Design Patterns for Microservices (Chen et al., 2021) - focus on service decomposition and interface design
Online resource: OpenAPI Specification Documentation (swagger.io) - complete specification guide and examples
Online resource: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (IETF RFC) - authentication flow implementations
Tutorial series: Postman Learning Center - API testing and documentation practices

title: Electric Circuits and Ohm's Law
description: This module introduces students to the fundamental principles of electric circuits, focusing on current, voltage, resistance, and their relationships through Ohm's Law. Students will explore both series and parallel circuit configurations while developing practical skills in circuit analysis and problem-solving. The module bridges theoretical understanding with hands-on experimentation, enabling students to construct and analyze real circuits using resistors, batteries, and measuring instruments. Through interactive simulations and laboratory work, students will gain confidence in applying circuit analysis techniques to everyday electrical devices. This foundation is essential for understanding more complex electrical phenomena and serves as a stepping stone to advanced topics in electromagnetism, electronics, and electrical engineering. The module emphasizes both mathematical modeling and physical intuition, helping students develop a robust understanding of how electrical energy flows through conducting materials and how circuit components interact to control current flow.
key_concepts: Electric current - the flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A)
Voltage (potential difference) - the electrical energy per unit charge that drives current flow, measured in volts (V)
Resistance - the opposition to current flow in a material, measured in ohms (Ω)
Ohm's Law - the fundamental relationship V = IR connecting voltage, current, and resistance
Series circuits - components connected end-to-end in a single path where current is constant throughout
Parallel circuits - components connected across common points where voltage is constant across branches
learning_objectives: Students will calculate current, voltage, and resistance in series and parallel circuits by applying Ohm's Law and Kirchhoff's circuit rules
Students will construct and analyze DC circuits through hands-on laboratory experiments using multimeters, resistors, and power sources
Students will predict circuit behavior and troubleshoot electrical problems using circuit simulation software and theoretical analysis
suggested_readings: University Physics: Chapter 25 - Current, Resistance, and Electromotive Force (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 822-855
Journal article: Teaching Circuit Analysis Through Interactive Simulations (Physics Education, 2019) - focus on pedagogical approaches
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Circuit Construction Kit: DC module with guided tutorials

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Uncovering Patterns and Insights
description: This module introduces students to the critical practice of Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), a fundamental step in any data science project that involves systematically examining datasets to discover patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses before formal statistical analysis. EDA serves as the bridge between raw data and meaningful insights, combining statistical techniques with data visualization to tell compelling stories from data. Students will learn to approach unfamiliar datasets methodically, using both descriptive statistics and visualization tools to understand data structure, identify relationships between variables, and spot potential data quality issues. The module emphasizes hands-on practice with real-world datasets, teaching students to ask the right questions, choose appropriate analytical techniques, and communicate findings effectively. By mastering EDA techniques, students develop critical thinking skills essential for data-driven decision making and build confidence in handling messy, real-world data scenarios that don't fit textbook examples.
key_concepts: Descriptive Statistics: Summary measures including central tendency, variability, and distribution shape that provide initial dataset understanding
Data Distribution Analysis: Examining how values are spread across variables using histograms, box plots, and probability plots to identify skewness and outliers
Correlation and Association: Measuring and visualizing relationships between variables using correlation coefficients, scatter plots, and contingency tables
Data Quality Assessment: Identifying missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, and logical errors that could impact analysis validity
Visual Storytelling: Creating clear, purposeful charts and graphs that effectively communicate findings to both technical and non-technical audiences
learning_objectives: Students will systematically examine unfamiliar datasets by applying the five-step EDA framework (Question, Wrangle, Explore, Draw Insights, Communicate)
Students will identify data patterns, outliers, and relationships through creating and interpreting univariate, bivariate, and multivariate visualizations using Python/R
Students will assess data quality and detect anomalies using descriptive statistics, distribution analysis, and correlation matrices
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' from Python for Data Analysis by Wes McKinney (2022) pp. 245-289
Journal article: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' by John Tukey (1977) - foundational principles and philosophy
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA course modules 1-4 focusing on data visualization and summary statistics techniques

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python: Uncovering Insights Through Visualization and Statistical Analysis
description: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the critical first step in any data science project, serving as the foundation for all subsequent modeling and analysis. This module provides hands-on experience with systematic data exploration techniques using Python's powerful visualization and statistical libraries. Students will learn to identify patterns, detect anomalies, test assumptions, and formulate hypotheses through interactive data exploration. The module emphasizes practical skills including data profiling, univariate and bivariate analysis, correlation detection, and outlier identification. Through real-world datasets from various domains (finance, healthcare, marketing), students will develop the analytical mindset necessary to extract meaningful insights before applying machine learning algorithms. This module bridges the gap between data cleaning and predictive modeling, ensuring students understand their data thoroughly before making analytical decisions. By the end of this module, students will possess a systematic framework for approaching any new dataset with confidence and rigor.
key_concepts: Data Profiling: Systematic examination of data structure, completeness, and quality metrics to understand dataset characteristics
Univariate Analysis: Statistical analysis of individual variables including distribution shape, central tendency, and variability measures
Bivariate Analysis: Examination of relationships between two variables using correlation coefficients, contingency tables, and comparative visualizations
Outlier Detection: Statistical and visual methods to identify data points that deviate significantly from expected patterns
Feature Relationships: Understanding how variables interact, including linear/non-linear correlations and categorical associations
learning_objectives: Students will perform comprehensive univariate analysis by creating distribution plots, summary statistics, and identifying data quality issues using pandas and matplotlib
Students will detect relationships and patterns in multivariate data through correlation matrices, scatter plots, and cross-tabulations using seaborn and plotly
Students will identify outliers and anomalies using statistical methods including IQR, z-scores, and isolation forests with scikit-learn
Students will formulate data-driven hypotheses and business insights by synthesizing findings from multiple exploratory techniques into actionable recommendations
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' from Python for Data Analysis by Wes McKinney (2022) pp. 245-289
Research article: 'The Art of Effective Visualization of Multi-dimensional Data' by Kumar & Singh (2023) - focus on EDA visualization principles
Online resource: Kaggle Learn - 'Data Visualization' course modules 1-4 covering matplotlib, seaborn, and plotly fundamentals
Case study: 'EDA Best Practices for Business Analytics' from Harvard Business Review Data Science collection (2023)

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) Fundamentals
description: Exploratory Data Analysis forms the critical foundation of any data science project, serving as the bridge between raw data and meaningful insights. This module equips students with systematic approaches to investigate datasets before applying complex statistical models or machine learning algorithms. Students will master the art of asking the right questions about data, identifying patterns, anomalies, and relationships that inform subsequent analysis decisions. The module emphasizes hands-on practice with real-world datasets, teaching students to combine statistical thinking with visual storytelling. By the end of this module, students will confidently approach unfamiliar datasets with a structured methodology, knowing how to clean, summarize, and visualize data effectively. This foundational skill is essential across all data analysis domains, from business intelligence to scientific research, making it one of the most transferable and valuable competencies in the data analyst's toolkit.
key_concepts: Data profiling - systematic examination of data quality, completeness, and structure to understand dataset characteristics
Univariate analysis - statistical and visual exploration of individual variables including distribution shapes, central tendencies, and outlier detection
Bivariate and multivariate analysis - investigation of relationships between variables using correlation analysis, cross-tabulations, and comparative visualizations
Data visualization principles - application of design principles to create clear, accurate, and compelling visual representations of data patterns
Missing data patterns - identification and analysis of missing data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and their implications for analysis strategies
learning_objectives: Students will execute a complete EDA workflow on messy real-world datasets by applying systematic data profiling, cleaning, and initial analysis techniques
Students will identify and interpret key patterns, outliers, and relationships in datasets through creation of appropriate statistical summaries and visualizations
Students will construct compelling data narratives using Python/R visualization libraries to communicate preliminary findings to both technical and non-technical audiences
suggested_readings: Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and IPython (McKinney, 2022) Chapter 7: Data Cleaning and Preparation, pp. 191-234
Journal article: The Split-Apply-Combine Strategy for Data Analysis (Wickham, 2011) - focus on data manipulation frameworks
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA Course - hands-on exercises with guided practice datasets
R for Data Science: Exploratory Data Analysis (Wickham & Grolemund, 2023) Chapter 7, pp. 141-168

title: Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems Through Matrix Methods
description: This module introduces students to systems of linear equations and their practical applications across various fields including economics, engineering, and data science. Students will master multiple solution methods, from graphical interpretation to advanced matrix techniques, while developing critical thinking skills to model real-world scenarios mathematically. The module emphasizes both computational proficiency and conceptual understanding, bridging the gap between abstract mathematical theory and tangible problem-solving. Students will explore how linear systems appear in supply chain optimization, traffic flow analysis, and investment portfolio balancing. By the end of this module, learners will confidently identify when linear systems are appropriate tools, construct systems from word problems, and select the most efficient solution method based on system characteristics. This foundational knowledge serves as a gateway to advanced topics in linear algebra, optimization theory, and mathematical modeling, making it essential for students pursuing STEM careers or quantitative analysis roles.
key_concepts: Linear equation: An equation of the form ax + by = c where variables appear only to the first power
Augmented matrix: A matrix formed by appending the constant terms of a system to the coefficient matrix for efficient computation
Gaussian elimination: A systematic method using elementary row operations to transform a system into row echelon form
Solution types: Unique solution (intersecting lines), no solution (parallel lines), or infinitely many solutions (coincident lines)
Matrix inverse method: Solving systems of the form AX = B by computing X = A⁻¹B when the coefficient matrix is invertible
learning_objectives: Students will solve 2x2 and 3x3 systems of linear equations by applying substitution, elimination, and matrix methods with 90% accuracy
Students will construct mathematical models from real-world scenarios through systematic analysis of constraints and variables in business and engineering contexts
Students will classify systems as consistent, inconsistent, or dependent using graphical analysis and augmented matrix row operations
suggested_readings: College Algebra textbook: Chapter 7 'Systems of Equations and Inequalities' (Blitzer, 2021) pp. 298-356
Journal article: 'Applications of Linear Systems in Supply Chain Management' (Operations Research Quarterly, 2022) - focuses on inventory optimization models
Khan Academy online: 'Systems of Linear Equations' modules - interactive practice problems with immediate feedback

title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Uncovering Patterns Through Statistical Visualization
description: This module focuses on Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), a critical first step in any data analysis project that involves systematically examining datasets to understand their structure, identify patterns, and detect anomalies before formal modeling. Students will learn to apply both statistical techniques and visualization methods to extract meaningful insights from raw data. EDA serves as the foundation for hypothesis generation and guides subsequent analytical decisions. Through hands-on practice with real datasets, students will master the art of asking the right questions about data, selecting appropriate visualization techniques, and interpreting statistical summaries. This module emphasizes practical skills including handling missing data, identifying outliers, understanding variable relationships, and communicating findings effectively. Students will work with both univariate and multivariate analysis techniques, learning when and how to apply different approaches based on data types and research objectives. By the end of this module, students will possess a systematic framework for approaching new datasets and the technical skills to implement comprehensive exploratory analyses that inform sound analytical strategies.
key_concepts: Descriptive Statistics: Measures of central tendency, variability, and distribution shape that summarize key characteristics of individual variables
Data Distribution Analysis: Understanding normal and non-normal distributions, skewness, kurtosis, and their implications for subsequent analysis
Correlation vs. Causation: Distinguishing between statistical association and causal relationships while identifying potential confounding variables
Outlier Detection: Statistical and visual methods for identifying extreme values and determining their impact on analysis
Missing Data Patterns: Systematic examination of missing data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and their analytical implications
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive univariate analysis by calculating descriptive statistics, creating appropriate visualizations, and identifying data quality issues for different variable types
Students will analyze relationships between multiple variables through correlation analysis, cross-tabulations, and multivariate visualizations to identify patterns and potential confounding factors
Students will implement systematic EDA workflows using Python/R to generate reproducible exploratory reports that guide hypothesis formation and analytical strategy decisions

Journal article: 'Exploratory Data Analysis in the 21st Century' (Yu & Kumbier, 2020) - focus on modern EDA techniques and computational approaches
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA Course - modules on data visualization and statistical analysis with interactive coding exercises

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) for Pattern Discovery
description: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the critical first step in any data analysis project, serving as the bridge between raw data and meaningful insights. This module focuses on systematic approaches to understanding data structure, identifying patterns, detecting anomalies, and formulating hypotheses before formal statistical modeling. Students will learn to combine statistical summaries with powerful visualization techniques to uncover hidden relationships in datasets. The module emphasizes practical skills using Python libraries (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn) and R for comprehensive data exploration. Through hands-on exercises with real-world datasets, students will develop the analytical mindset necessary to ask the right questions, recognize data quality issues, and communicate preliminary findings effectively. This foundational skill set is essential for data scientists, analysts, and researchers across all industries, as proper EDA often determines the success of subsequent analysis phases and prevents costly modeling errors.
key_concepts: Data Profiling - Systematic examination of data quality, completeness, and structure to understand dataset characteristics
Statistical Summaries - Measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape that describe data numerically

Outlier Detection - Methods for identifying anomalous data points that may indicate errors or important exceptions
Data Visualization Grammar - Principles for selecting appropriate chart types and visual encodings based on data types and analytical goals
