Research article: 'The Future of Data Analysis' by Tukey (1962) - foundational EDA philosophy and methodology
Online resource: Kaggle Learn EDA course modules - hands-on exercises with guided datasets
Documentation: Seaborn statistical visualization library - comprehensive plotting techniques for EDA

title: Newton's Laws of Motion: Forces and Dynamics
description: This module provides a comprehensive exploration of Newton's three laws of motion, forming the foundation of classical mechanics and our understanding of how forces affect object motion. Students will transition from conceptual understanding to quantitative problem-solving, learning to analyze real-world scenarios involving forces, acceleration, and momentum. The module emphasizes the interconnected nature of Newton's laws through hands-on experiments, mathematical modeling, and practical applications ranging from everyday experiences like walking and driving to engineering applications in aerospace and automotive design. By connecting abstract principles to observable phenomena, students develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced physics topics including energy conservation, rotational dynamics, and fluid mechanics. This module serves as a crucial bridge between kinematics and more complex mechanical systems, establishing the analytical framework students will use throughout their physics education and potential careers in STEM fields.
key_concepts: Inertia - An object's resistance to changes in motion, directly related to mass and fundamental to Newton's First Law
Net Force - The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, determining acceleration according to F = ma
Action-Reaction Pairs - Equal and opposite forces between interacting objects as described by Newton's Third Law
Free-Body Diagrams - Graphical representations isolating an object and showing all forces acting upon it
Equilibrium - The state when net force equals zero, resulting in constant velocity or rest
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex force systems by applying Newton's three laws to solve multi-step dynamics problems involving friction, tension, and normal forces
Students will predict and verify object motion through laboratory experiments using force sensors, motion detectors, and video analysis software
Students will construct free-body diagrams using vector notation to represent and calculate net forces in two-dimensional scenarios
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 5: Applying Newton's Laws (Young & Freedman, 2019) pp. 124-158
Research article: Teaching Newton's Laws Through Interactive Demonstrations (McDermott, 2018) - focus on misconception identification
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Forces and Motion: Basics simulation with guided worksheet
Supplementary: Khan Academy Physics - Newton's Laws section videos 1-6 for concept reinforcement

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD): Building Reliable Software Through Testing First
description: This module introduces Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that prioritizes writing tests before implementing functionality. Students will learn the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, understand how TDD influences design decisions, and practice writing effective unit tests using modern testing frameworks. The module emphasizes hands-on coding exercises where students experience the iterative nature of TDD and discover how this approach leads to more maintainable, bug-free code. Students will work with real-world scenarios, learning to write meaningful test cases that drive implementation decisions and serve as living documentation. By the end of this module, students will understand when and how to apply TDD principles, recognize the benefits of test-first development for code quality and team collaboration, and be able to implement TDD workflows in their own projects using industry-standard tools and practices.
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The core TDD workflow of writing a failing test (Red), implementing minimal code to pass (Green), and improving the design (Refactor)
Unit Testing: Writing isolated tests that verify individual functions or methods work correctly, forming the foundation of the TDD approach
Test Coverage and Quality: Understanding the difference between line coverage metrics and meaningful test scenarios that actually validate business logic
Refactoring: The practice of improving code structure and readability without changing external behavior, enabled by comprehensive test suites
Mocking and Stubbing: Techniques for isolating units under test by replacing dependencies with controlled test doubles
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor cycle by writing failing tests, making them pass, and improving code structure through guided coding exercises
Students will evaluate code quality and design decisions through analyzing TDD-developed versus traditionally-developed codebases in comparative case studies
Students will create comprehensive unit test suites using Jest and Python unittest frameworks for both new features and legacy code refactoring scenarios
suggested_readings: Test-Driven Development: By Example - Kent Beck (2002) Chapters 1-8, pp. 1-89
Journal article: The Effects of Test-Driven Development on External Quality and Productivity (Siniaalto & Abrahamsson, 2007) - focus on empirical results
Online resource: Jest Documentation - Getting Started and Testing Asynchronous Code sections
Martin Fowler's blog: Test-Driven Development article and Mocks Aren't Stubs - practical implementation guidance

title: Big O Notation and Algorithm Complexity Analysis
description: This module introduces students to algorithm complexity analysis using Big O notation, a fundamental concept for evaluating algorithm efficiency. Students will learn to analyze time and space complexity of algorithms, enabling them to make informed decisions when selecting or designing algorithms for real-world problems. The module covers mathematical foundations of asymptotic notation, practical analysis techniques for common algorithm patterns (loops, recursion, divide-and-conquer), and comparative analysis of data structures. Through hands-on coding exercises and complexity calculations, students will develop the analytical skills necessary to predict algorithm performance at scale. This knowledge is essential for technical interviews, system design, and building efficient software solutions. The module emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical application, preparing students to optimize code performance and communicate algorithm trade-offs effectively in professional settings.
key_concepts: Big O Notation: Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
Time Complexity: Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
Space Complexity: Analysis of memory usage required by an algorithm including auxiliary space and input storage
Asymptotic Analysis: Mathematical framework for describing algorithm behavior with very large inputs
Best/Average/Worst Case: Different scenarios of algorithm performance based on input characteristics and distribution
learning_objectives: Students will calculate time and space complexity for iterative and recursive algorithms by applying Big O, Omega, and Theta notation rules
Students will compare algorithm efficiency across different input sizes through empirical testing and mathematical analysis
Students will optimize existing code implementations using complexity analysis to identify bottlenecks and select appropriate data structures
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: Introduction to Algorithms, Ch 3 'Growth of Functions' (Cormen et al., 2022) pp. 43-68
Journal article: 'Teaching Algorithm Analysis: A Practical Approach' (Smith, 2023) - focus on pedagogical methods and common misconceptions
Online resource: Khan Academy - 'Asymptotic Notation' interactive lessons with visualization tools
Supplementary: GeeksforGeeks 'Analysis of Algorithms' tutorials - practical examples and code implementations

title: Advanced Data Structures: Binary Trees and Balanced Trees
description: This module provides an in-depth exploration of tree-based data structures, focusing on binary trees, binary search trees (BSTs), and self-balancing trees including AVL and Red-Black trees. Students will master the theoretical foundations of these hierarchical data structures while developing practical implementation skills. The module emphasizes understanding time and space complexity trade-offs, tree traversal algorithms, and the critical importance of maintaining balance for optimal performance. Through hands-on coding exercises and algorithmic analysis, students will learn when and why to choose specific tree structures for different applications. This knowledge is essential for efficient database indexing, compiler design, file systems, and many other computer science applications. The module bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical software development skills, preparing students for advanced algorithms courses and real-world programming challenges where efficient data organization and retrieval are paramount.
key_concepts: Binary Search Tree (BST) - A hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, with left subtree values less than parent and right subtree values greater than parent
Tree Traversal Algorithms - Systematic methods for visiting all nodes in a tree: inorder (left-root-right), preorder (root-left-right), postorder (left-right-root), and level-order (breadth-first)
AVL Tree Balancing - Self-balancing binary search tree where heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most one, maintained through rotations
Tree Rotations - Local restructuring operations (single and double rotations) that preserve BST property while improving balance
Red-Black Tree Properties - Self-balancing BST with color-coded nodes following specific rules to guarantee O(log n) operations
learning_objectives: Students will implement binary search trees with insertion, deletion, and search operations by writing complete Java or Python classes with proper error handling
Students will analyze tree traversal algorithms (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order) through both recursive and iterative implementations
Students will design and implement AVL tree rotations and rebalancing algorithms using step-by-step visual debugging techniques
Students will evaluate time complexity scenarios for balanced vs unbalanced trees by conducting empirical performance analysis with datasets of varying sizes
Students will solve real-world problems requiring tree data structures through project-based assignments involving file system simulation or expression parsing
suggested_readings: Introduction to Algorithms: Chapter 12 'Binary Search Trees' and Chapter 13 'Red-Black Trees' (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein, 4th Edition) pp. 287-348
Journal article: 'An algorithm for the organization of information' (Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 1962) - historical foundation of AVL trees
Online resource: VisuAlgo.net - Interactive Binary Search Tree and AVL Tree visualizations with step-by-step algorithm execution
Supplementary reading: 'Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis' Chapter 4 'Trees' (Weiss, 4th Edition) pp. 131-186

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Implementation and Practices
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing code. TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, where developers first write failing tests (Red), implement minimal code to pass tests (Green), and then improve code quality while maintaining functionality (Refactor). This approach fundamentally changes how developers think about code design, leading to more modular, testable, and maintainable software. Students will learn to write effective unit tests, understand test coverage metrics, and apply TDD principles to real-world programming scenarios. The module emphasizes practical application through hands-on coding exercises using popular testing frameworks. By mastering TDD, students develop disciplined coding habits, improve debugging skills, and create more reliable software systems. This methodology is widely adopted in agile development environments and is considered essential for modern software engineering practices. Students will also explore how TDD integrates with continuous integration pipelines and contributes to overall software quality assurance processes.
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests, implementing minimal code to pass, and improving code structure
Unit Testing: Automated tests that verify individual components or functions in isolation from the rest of the system
Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, typically expressed as a percentage
Test Doubles: Mock objects, stubs, and fakes used to isolate units under test from their dependencies
Refactoring: The process of restructuring existing code without changing its external behavior to improve readability and maintainability
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor cycle by writing failing tests, minimal passing code, and refactored solutions for at least three programming problems
Students will analyze code quality improvements through hands-on comparison of TDD versus traditional development approaches using metrics like cyclomatic complexity and test coverage
Students will create comprehensive unit test suites using JUnit (Java) or pytest (Python) frameworks for a medium-complexity application with at least 80% code coverage
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Test-Driven Development' in Clean Code by Robert Martin (2008) pp. 123-142
Research article: 'On the Effectiveness of Test-first Approach to Programming' by Erdogmus et al. (2005) - empirical evidence for TDD benefits
Online resource: Kent Beck's Test-Driven Development tutorial series on Martin Fowler's website - practical TDD examples and best practices
Documentation: JUnit 5 User Guide sections 1-4 or pytest documentation chapters 1-3 depending on chosen language

title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Feature Engineering
description: This module focuses on the critical phase of data science where raw data is transformed into actionable insights and prepared for modeling. Students will master the art and science of exploring datasets to uncover hidden patterns, identify data quality issues, and engineer meaningful features that enhance model performance. The module emphasizes both statistical techniques and practical Python implementations using pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn. Students will learn to ask the right questions about their data, visualize distributions and relationships, handle missing values strategically, and create new variables that capture domain knowledge. This foundational skill set is essential for any data science project, as poor EDA often leads to flawed models regardless of algorithmic sophistication. The module combines theoretical understanding with hands-on practice using real-world datasets from various domains including healthcare, finance, and e-commerce.
key_concepts: Univariate Analysis - Statistical summaries, distribution shapes, and central tendency measures for individual variables
Bivariate Analysis - Correlation analysis, scatter plots, and relationship identification between variable pairs
Feature Engineering - Creating new variables through mathematical transformations, binning, and domain-specific calculations
Data Quality Assessment - Missing value patterns, outlier detection methods, and data consistency validation
Categorical Encoding - One-hot encoding, label encoding, and target encoding techniques for non-numeric variables
learning_objectives: Students will conduct comprehensive exploratory data analysis by implementing statistical summaries, distribution analysis, and correlation studies using pandas and matplotlib
Students will identify and address data quality issues through systematic missing value analysis, outlier detection, and data validation techniques
Students will engineer meaningful features using domain knowledge, mathematical transformations, and encoding techniques for categorical variables
Students will create compelling data visualizations through seaborn and matplotlib to communicate insights to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
suggested_readings: Python for Data Analysis: Chapter 7-9 Data Cleaning and Preparation (McKinney, 2017) pp. 195-267
Journal article: Feature Engineering for Machine Learning: Principles and Techniques (Zheng & Casari, 2018) - Chapters 2-4 focus
Online resource: Kaggle Learn - Data Visualization and Feature Engineering modules with interactive exercises

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): Uncovering Patterns Through Visualization and Statistical Summaries
description: This module focuses on Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), a critical initial phase in any data analysis project where analysts examine datasets to understand their structure, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and formulate hypotheses for further investigation. Students will learn to systematically approach unfamiliar datasets using both statistical summaries and data visualization techniques. The module emphasizes the iterative nature of EDA, where initial observations lead to deeper questions and more targeted analyses. Through hands-on practice with real-world datasets, students will develop intuition for recognizing data quality issues, understanding variable relationships, and communicating preliminary findings to stakeholders. This foundational skill set is essential for making informed decisions about subsequent modeling approaches and ensuring data integrity throughout the analysis pipeline. The module balances theoretical understanding with practical application, using industry-standard tools to prepare students for professional data analysis roles.
key_concepts: Descriptive Statistics: Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and variability (standard deviation, IQR) that summarize dataset characteristics
Data Distribution Analysis: Understanding variable distributions through histograms, density plots, and normality tests to inform modeling decisions
Correlation and Association: Measuring linear relationships between continuous variables and dependencies between categorical variables using correlation coefficients and contingency tables
Outlier Detection: Identifying extreme values through statistical methods (z-scores, IQR method) and visual inspection that may indicate errors or important insights
Missing Data Patterns: Analyzing patterns of missingness (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and their implications for analysis validity
learning_objectives: Students will systematically evaluate dataset characteristics and quality by computing descriptive statistics, identifying missing values, and detecting outliers using Python pandas and numpy libraries

Students will create and interpret comprehensive data visualizations through constructing histograms, box plots, scatter plots, and correlation matrices to reveal distribution patterns and variable relationships
Students will formulate data-driven hypotheses using structured EDA frameworks to guide subsequent analysis phases and communicate findings through written summaries and visual presentations
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' from Python for Data Analysis by McKinney (2022) pp. 267-312
Journal article: 'Exploratory Data Analysis' by Tukey (1977) - foundational concepts and philosophy of EDA approach
Online resource: Kaggle Learn - Data Visualization course modules 1-3 focusing on matplotlib and seaborn implementation

title: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Laws
description: This module explores the fundamental relationship between changing magnetic fields and induced electric currents, forming the cornerstone of modern electrical technology. Students will investigate Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and Lenz's law through both theoretical analysis and hands-on experimentation. The module begins with the concept of magnetic flux and progresses through induced EMF, self-inductance, and mutual inductance. Practical applications including electric generators, transformers, and induction motors are examined to demonstrate real-world relevance. Students will conduct laboratory experiments using bar magnets, solenoids, and galvanometers to observe electromagnetic induction firsthand. Mathematical problem-solving focuses on calculating induced EMF, determining the direction of induced currents, and analyzing energy transformations in electromagnetic systems. This module bridges the gap between static electric and magnetic phenomena covered in earlier units and the dynamic electromagnetic wave theory that follows. Understanding electromagnetic induction is essential for comprehending how most of our electrical power infrastructure operates, from power plant generators to household transformers.
key_concepts: Magnetic flux: The measure of magnetic field lines passing through a given surface area, calculated as Φ = B⃗ · A⃗ = BA cos θ
Faraday's law: The induced EMF in a closed loop equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop, ε = -dΦ/dt
Lenz's law: The direction of induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change causing the induction
Self-inductance: The property of a circuit element that opposes changes in current through itself, characterized by L = Φ/I
Motional EMF: The EMF induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field, ε = BLv for a straight conductor
learning_objectives: Students will calculate induced EMF in various geometric configurations by applying Faraday's law to problems involving changing magnetic flux
Students will predict the direction of induced currents through systematic application of Lenz's law to electromagnetic scenarios
Students will analyze the operation of transformers and generators using electromagnetic induction principles and energy conservation laws
Students will demonstrate electromagnetic induction phenomena through laboratory experiments with coils, magnets, and measuring instruments
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 29: Electromagnetic Induction (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 950-985
Journal article: Modern Applications of Electromagnetic Induction (Chen, 2019) - focus on wireless charging technology
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - Faraday's Law simulation and accompanying guided activities

title: Wave Interference and Diffraction
description: This module explores the fascinating wave behaviors of interference and diffraction, fundamental phenomena that demonstrate the wave nature of light, sound, and matter. Students will investigate how waves interact when they meet, creating patterns of constructive and destructive interference, and how waves bend around obstacles and through openings. These concepts are crucial for understanding modern technologies including noise-canceling headphones, optical instruments, X-ray crystallography, and quantum mechanics. Through hands-on experiments with water waves, sound waves, and laser light, students will develop both conceptual understanding and mathematical skills needed to predict and analyze wave patterns. The module emphasizes real-world applications from architectural acoustics to medical imaging, showing how wave interference principles impact daily life and cutting-edge research. Students will use both analytical methods and computer simulations to model complex wave behaviors, preparing them for advanced topics in optics, acoustics, and quantum physics.
key_concepts: Superposition Principle - waves add algebraically when they overlap, creating regions of reinforcement and cancellation
Path Difference - the difference in distances traveled by two waves from their sources to a point, determining interference type
Coherence - the degree to which waves maintain constant phase relationships, essential for observable interference patterns
Single-slit Diffraction - bending and spreading of waves through narrow openings, creating characteristic intensity patterns
Double-slit Interference - alternating bright and dark fringes created when coherent waves pass through two parallel slits
Diffraction Grating - optical device with many parallel slits that disperses light into component wavelengths through interference
learning_objectives: Students will calculate the positions of constructive and destructive interference maxima and minima by applying the path difference formula and wave superposition principle
Students will predict diffraction patterns for single-slit and circular apertures through mathematical analysis using the Rayleigh criterion and Fresnel number
Students will design and conduct interference experiments using laser pointers, double-slits, and diffraction gratings to measure wavelengths and validate theoretical predictions
suggested_readings: University Physics: Chapter 35 'Interference' and Chapter 36 'Diffraction' (Young & Freedman, 2019) pp. 1162-1242
Journal article: 'Visualizing Wave Interference with Digital Photography' (American Journal of Physics, 2020) - experimental techniques focus
Online resource: PhET Interactive Simulations - 'Wave Interference' and 'Single Slit Diffraction' modules with guided worksheets

title: Wave Interference and Superposition Phenomena
description: This module explores the fundamental principles of wave interference and superposition, examining how waves interact when they overlap in space and time. Students will investigate constructive and destructive interference patterns, standing waves, and beats through both theoretical analysis and practical applications. The module emphasizes the mathematical framework of wave superposition while connecting these concepts to real-world phenomena such as noise-canceling headphones, musical acoustics, and optical interference patterns. Through hands-on experiments with water waves, sound waves, and light waves, students will develop a deep understanding of how the principle of superposition governs wave behavior across all physical systems. This foundation is crucial for understanding advanced topics in optics, quantum mechanics, and electromagnetic theory. The module balances conceptual understanding with quantitative problem-solving skills, preparing students to analyze complex wave systems in engineering and scientific applications.
key_concepts: Principle of Superposition - waves combine algebraically when overlapping, with the resultant displacement being the sum of individual wave displacements
Constructive Interference - waves combine to produce maximum amplitude when their phase difference is zero or multiples of 2π
Destructive Interference - waves cancel partially or completely when their phase difference is π or odd multiples of π
Standing Waves - stationary wave patterns formed by interference between incident and reflected waves with fixed nodes and antinodes
Beat Phenomenon - periodic amplitude variations resulting from superposition of two waves with slightly different frequencies
learning_objectives: Students will calculate interference patterns and wave amplitudes by applying the mathematical principle of superposition to overlapping sinusoidal waves
Students will predict and analyze standing wave formations through experimental manipulation of string tensions, frequencies, and boundary conditions
Students will determine beat frequencies and interference conditions using wave equation analysis and graphical wave representation techniques
suggested_readings: University Physics Chapter 16: Wave Interference (Young & Freedman, 2020) pp. 512-547
Journal article: Visualizing Wave Interference Patterns in Multiple Media (American Journal of Physics, 2019) - experimental techniques and analysis methods
Online resource: PhET Wave Interference Simulation - interactive wave superposition and interference pattern generation
Supplementary reading: Principles of Physics Chapter 14.4-14.6 (Halliday, Resnick & Walker, 2018) pp. 421-438

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) with JavaScript and Jest
description: This module introduces students to Test-Driven Development (TDD), a fundamental software development methodology that emphasizes writing tests before implementing functionality. Students will learn the Red-Green-Refactor cycle, understand different types of testing (unit, integration, and acceptance tests), and gain hands-on experience using Jest testing framework with JavaScript. The module covers essential testing concepts including test structure, assertions, mocking, and test coverage analysis. TDD is crucial for modern software development as it improves code quality, reduces debugging time, facilitates refactoring, and ensures comprehensive test coverage. Students will practice writing maintainable, well-documented tests and learn how TDD influences software design decisions. By the end of this module, students will understand how to approach development projects with a test-first mindset, create robust test suites, and integrate testing into their development workflow. This foundation prepares students for professional development environments where automated testing and continuous integration are standard practices.
key_concepts: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle: The three-phase TDD process of writing failing tests (Red), making tests pass (Green), and improving code structure (Refactor)
Test Coverage: Measurement of how much source code is executed during testing, including line, branch, and function coverage metrics
Test Doubles: Objects that replace dependencies during testing, including mocks, stubs, spies, and fakes to isolate units under test
Arrange-Act-Assert Pattern: Standard test structure that sets up test conditions (Arrange), executes the code being tested (Act), and verifies results (Assert)
Testable Design: Code architecture principles that make testing easier, including dependency injection, single responsibility, and loose coupling
learning_objectives: Students will implement the Red-Green-Refactor TDD cycle by writing failing tests first, making them pass with minimal code, and then refactoring for code quality
Students will create comprehensive test suites through hands-on coding exercises using Jest framework for unit and integration testing
Students will analyze and improve code quality using Jest's coverage reporting tools and test result analysis features
Students will design testable code architecture by applying dependency injection and modular programming principles learned through TDD practice
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Test-Driven Development by Example' (Beck, K., 2003) Chapters 1-3, pp. 1-45
Journal article: 'Does Test-Driven Development Really Improve Software Design Quality?' (Janzen & Saiedian, 2008) - focus on empirical evidence and design benefits
Online resource: Jest Documentation - Getting Started and API Reference sections at jestjs.io
Online resource: JavaScript Testing Best Practices (Goldbergs, Y., 2022) - TDD patterns and anti-patterns section
Code repository: TDD Kata exercises collection on GitHub - specific focus on String Calculator and FizzBuzz problems

title: Advanced SQL Query Optimization and Performance Tuning
description: This module focuses on the critical skills needed to write efficient SQL queries and optimize database performance in production environments. Students will learn to analyze query execution plans, identify performance bottlenecks, and implement optimization strategies that can dramatically improve application response times. The module covers indexing strategies, query rewriting techniques, and database-specific optimization features. With databases being the backbone of most software systems, understanding how to optimize SQL queries is essential for any computer science professional working with data-driven applications. Students will work with real-world datasets and use professional database management tools to measure performance improvements. By the end of this module, students will be able to transform slow-running queries into high-performance solutions and make informed decisions about database design that impact overall system scalability. This knowledge is immediately applicable to internships, capstone projects, and professional software development roles.
key_concepts: Query Execution Plans - Visual representations showing how the database engine processes SQL statements, including operation costs and data flow
Index Selectivity - A measure of how unique values are in an indexed column, directly affecting query performance and index effectiveness
Join Algorithms - Different strategies (nested loop, hash join, merge join) used by databases to combine data from multiple tables
Query Rewriting - Techniques for transforming logically equivalent queries into more efficient forms without changing results
Database Statistics - Metadata about data distribution that query optimizers use to choose the best execution strategy
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by interpreting cost estimates, join strategies, and index usage patterns using database profiling tools
Students will optimize poorly performing queries through hands-on refactoring exercises that demonstrate measurable performance improvements
Students will design and implement appropriate indexing strategies using B-tree, hash, and composite indexes based on query patterns and data characteristics
suggested_readings: Database System Concepts: Chapter 13 'Query Optimization' (Silberschatz, Galvin, Gagne, 7th Edition) pp. 521-580
Research paper: 'Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System' (Selinger et al., 1979) - foundational query optimization algorithms
Online resource: PostgreSQL Documentation - Query Planning and Performance Tips sections with execution plan examples
Technical article: 'Use The Index, Luke!' - SQL Performance Explained (winand.at) - indexing strategies and anti-patterns

title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python: Uncovering Insights Before Modeling
description: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is a critical foundation skill in data science that involves systematically examining datasets to understand their structure, patterns, and anomalies before applying machine learning models. This module teaches students how to approach unfamiliar datasets methodically, identify data quality issues, discover hidden relationships between variables, and generate actionable hypotheses for further investigation. Students will master both statistical and visual techniques using Python's pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries to transform raw data into meaningful insights. The module emphasizes real-world application through hands-on analysis of messy, authentic datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, and social media. By the end of this module, students will possess a systematic framework for conducting thorough exploratory analysis, enabling them to make informed decisions about data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model selection in subsequent data science projects.
key_concepts: Univariate Analysis: Statistical examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
Bivariate Analysis: Investigation of relationships between two variables using correlation coefficients, scatter plots, and cross-tabulations
Data Profiling: Systematic assessment of data quality including completeness, consistency, accuracy, and validity checks
Outlier Detection: Statistical and visual methods for identifying anomalous data points using IQR, Z-scores, and box plots
Feature Distribution Analysis: Understanding variable distributions through histograms, density plots, and Q-Q plots to inform preprocessing decisions
learning_objectives: Students will systematically examine dataset structure and quality by implementing a comprehensive EDA checklist covering data types, missing values, duplicates, and distribution analysis
Students will identify significant patterns and relationships between variables through creating correlation matrices, scatter plots, and statistical summaries using pandas and seaborn

Students will generate actionable business insights and testable hypotheses using advanced visualization techniques including pair plots, heatmaps, and multi-dimensional charts with matplotlib and seaborn
suggested_readings: Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with Pandas, NumPy, and IPython (McKinney, 2022) pp. 145-210
Journal article: The Role of Exploratory Data Analysis in Data Science Workflows (Zhang et al., 2023) - focus on systematic EDA methodology
Kaggle Learn: Data Visualization course - modules on statistical plotting and advanced seaborn techniques
Online resource: Towards Data Science - 'A Comprehensive Guide to EDA with Python' including code templates and best practices

title: API Design and RESTful Web Services
description: This module focuses on designing, building, and consuming Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) using REST architectural principles. Students will learn to create scalable, maintainable web services that enable communication between different software systems. The module covers fundamental REST concepts, HTTP methods, status codes, authentication mechanisms, and best practices for API versioning and documentation. Through hands-on exercises, students will design API endpoints, implement CRUD operations, handle error responses, and test their APIs using industry-standard tools. This knowledge is essential for modern software development, as APIs serve as the backbone for web applications, mobile apps, microservices architectures, and third-party integrations. Students will gain practical experience with popular frameworks and tools while learning to evaluate trade-offs in API design decisions. The module emphasizes real-world scenarios including rate limiting, caching strategies, and security considerations that professional developers encounter daily.
key_concepts: REST (Representational State Transfer) - Architectural style for distributed systems emphasizing stateless communication and resource-based URLs
HTTP Methods - GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH operations that define actions performed on API resources
Status Codes - Standardized numeric codes (200, 404, 500, etc.) that communicate the outcome of API requests
JSON Web Tokens (JWT) - Compact, secure method for transmitting information between parties as digitally signed tokens
API Versioning - Strategies for managing changes to API interfaces while maintaining backward compatibility
Rate Limiting - Technique to control the number of requests a client can make within a specified time period
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) - Security mechanism that allows or restricts web applications from different domains to access API resources
learning_objectives: Students will design RESTful API endpoints following HTTP conventions by analyzing business requirements and mapping them to appropriate resource URIs and HTTP methods
Students will implement a complete CRUD API with proper error handling and status codes through building a backend service using Express.js and Node.js
Students will document and test APIs using OpenAPI specification and Postman by creating comprehensive API documentation and automated test suites
Students will evaluate API security measures and implement authentication mechanisms using JWT tokens and API key strategies
Students will analyze API performance considerations and apply caching and rate limiting techniques through implementing middleware solutions
suggested_readings: Textbook chapter: 'Building Web APIs' from Web Development with Node and Express (Brown, 2019) pp. 287-325
Research paper: 'REST: Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures' (Fielding, 2000) - Chapters 5-6 focusing on REST constraints
Online resource: MDN Web Docs - HTTP Methods and Status Codes comprehensive reference guide
Industry article: 'API Security Best Practices' from OWASP API Security Top 10 (2021) - Authentication and authorization sections
Documentation: OpenAPI Specification 3.0 - Schema definition and documentation standards
